Has the government taken action in response to the options set out in the "Environmental Quality Strategic Review: a follow-up report of the Task Force on Program Review", published on February 21, 1986 and, if so, for each option, what action has been taken?

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom McMillan (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext: Yes. The "Environmental Quality Strategic Review: a follow-up report of the Task Force on Program Review", was one of a number of task force reports that made recommendations on the programs of the Department of the Environment. No specific point by point response to the options set out in the "Environmental Quality Strategic Review" document is being planned but as a result of all the reports, the government has adopted an Environmental Quality Strategy which involves a number of initiatives. These include the new Canadian Environmental Protection Act; improvements in the management of federal efforts in the environmental sciences; the establishment of a federal "state of the environment" reporting system; and the further integration of environmental and economic decision making.

The House resumed from Thursday, November 26, consideration of the motion of Mr. Hnatyshyn that Bill C-54, an Act to amend the Criminal Code and other Acts in consequence thereof, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

Mr. Speaker, in the time remaining to me I want to bring to the attention of the House the extent of opposition to this legislation by a broad range of groups across Canada. During my opening remarks last Thursday, I indicated that certainly we in the NDP are prepared to accept legislation, indeed have called upon the Government for it, that would recognize the concern of Canadians particularly with respect to violence, degradation and child pornography. However, this legislation goes far beyond that in its attempt to control the depiction of imagery which involves neither violence, degradation nor child pornography. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) in his remarks last Thursday said:
All Hon. Members realize that the time has come to amend the Criminal
Code to deal with child pornography and with material which is sexually
violent, exploitative, and degrading.
This Bill does not deal just with that material. It deals with a broad range of other material as well. I pointed out that images of two adults engaged in consensual love-making would henceforth be illegal under the new regime in this legislation.
Who are some of the groups which have expressed concern about this Bill and what is the nature of their concern? The groups include ACTRA, the AIDS Committee of Toronto, the Canada Council, the Canadian Committee against Customs Censorship, the Canadian Conference of the Arts, the Book and Periodical Development Council, the Canadian Librarians' Association, Coalition for the Right to View, Media People for Social Responsibility, the National Action Committee on the Status of Women, the International Rights Organization PEN, and the Writers' Union of Canada, and indeed, a wide range of other organizations.
[DOT] (mo)
The Attorneys General of Canada have indicated their concern that the Bill is too sweeping. They are worried, as was suggested by the then Attorney General of Manitoba, Roland

Penner, that "to include the portrayal of normal, healthy sexual activity along with sexual violence and kiddie porn seems to indicate a misplaced sense of values". He said:
Every provincial minister who spoke advised the federal minister of justice
that they thought he has problems with that bill and he ought to take a closer
look.
The Attorneys General of Canada are asking the Minister of Justice to take another look at this important piece of legislation.
We have as well the position of the Canadian Library Association in addition to that of the British Columbia Teacher-Librarians' Association. The Canadian Library Association, a national non-profit organization representing some 4,500 librarians, indicates that it is deeply concerned about the provisions of Bill C-54. It states that Bill C-54 would require a radical reorganization of library services and operations.
It give some examples. It suggests that library collections would have to be separated into materials for clients over the age of 18 and under the age of 18, that substantial changes to material selection policy and screening processes would need to be undertaken to ensure that libraries are not criminally liable, and that library staff under the age of 18 could no longer be employed in an "adult library". Those are the general concerns of the Canadian Library Association.
I have also received, as has the Minister of Justice, a more detailed letter from the British Columbia Teacher-Librarians' Association. They say that a great deal of the teenage and young adult fiction and a great deal of our educational material would become suspect under this new Bill. They go on to indicate that many teenage and young adult novels deal in very real ways with the problems facing young people today, whether it is coming to terms with their own sexuality, dealing with sexual abuse, living in an alcoholic family, or attempting to establish a positive self image. They have information on venereal diseases such as AIDS, and on dealing with sexual abuse, rape, incest, and violence. They suggest that much of this material in their school libraries could become open to question under the Bill and that teacher-librarians could face criminal charges under the provisions of this legislation.
The onus under this Bill with regard to artists is on the artist to prove to the courts what is referred to as "artistic merit". It has been pointed out by a number of artists that it is a very dangerous proposal to put the burden on an artist to prove in some way that his or her art work has merit. Instead, surely the test should be the same as that for educational, scientific, and other works, and that is the purpose of the work rather than the extent of the merit of it. Judges are not in a position to evaluate the merit of artistic imagery. I suggest that the courts should be looking at the purpose of that work.
The implications of a test of merit are very different. If a judge does not find the artistry to be of top quality, although the work clearly had no purpose of a pornographic nature, he
could find those who distribute that art criminally liable under the provisions of this legislation.
The Bill before us already appears to be having some effect in school districts in British Columbia where groups such as Citizens for Human Dignity, are coming into schools, acquiring materials which they perceive to be pornographic, and threatening teacher-librarians and school boards with charges and lawsuits. Is this what we will be facing in the future under the provisions of this legislation? Will we see the kinds of attacks on literature that were made on the works of Margaret Laurence in a rural school board in Ontario? That is the kind of mentality which seems to be encouraged by this legislation. It is a very dangerous and Draconian approach to legislation.
The Canada Council, through its chairperson Maureen Forrester, has indicated that it has concerns about this legislation, particularly because of the possible implications under the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. The council points out that putting the onus on an artist to prove the merit of his or her work is very likely in breach of the provisions of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Miss Forrester indicates that she knows how worried artists and arts groups are about the implications of this Bill for their work. She says that the Canada Council shares their concerns.
The Planned Parenthood Federation of Canada has pointed out that this legislation appears to confuse healthy sexuality and disordered sexuality. They say that the legislation is fundamentally anti-sexual. It purports to include a definition of erotica which is nothing more and nothing less than nudity in a sexual context. However, the minute that there is any form of sexual contact it suddenly becomes pornographic and thus illegal. The Planned Parenthood Federation of Canada states that the proposed legislation will have a chilling effect on sexuality and reproductive education and research in Canada. That group has an excellent record in the area of sex education and promotion of more effective and better sex education and research.
Concerns about the scope of this legislation have been raised by a number of groups working with people with AIDS across Canada. The AIDS Committee of Toronto, for example, has stated:
We believe that Bill C-54, if passed in its present form, will have a devastating effect on the ability of our organization and of other AIDS and sex education organizations in Canada to provide the information which is vitally needed in the fight against this disease.
They are saying that if this Bill is passed it could have a very serious impact on preventive steps in the area of AIDS. They note as well that the great bulk of pornography as defined in this legislation depicts legal sexual activities, and that many of these materials are an important element of the preventive safe sex approach which is taken by groups such as the AIDS Committee of Toronto.
The AIDS Committee of Toronto is active in advocating safer sexual alternatives. The depiction of many of the alternatives which are advocated could be illegal under the
November 30, 1987

provisions of this legislation. As the AIDS Committee of Toronto points out, it should be evident from its submissions that any realistic attempt to reduce the spread of AIDS must include frank discussion of sexuality. Under the provisions of this legislation those kinds of discussions could be illegal and subject to prosecution.
Why should those who are working on the front lines against this terrible disease have to take the time, energy, and resources to prove that they have an educational or scientific defence for their work? That is the implication of this legislation.
Nonsense.

There are Conservative Members opposite who say that that is not the case. They will have an opportunity to stand and defend this legislation. However, the reality is that that is exactly what the implication of this legislation could be. We have heard it said in the past that legislation of this nature will not be abused. We are told that we should trust that the Crown will not be abusing it. However, it was not that long ago that the Supreme Court of Canada only narrowly ruled that the great work, Lady Chatterley's Lover, was not obscene.
As well, the AIDS Committee of Toronto and other individuals and groups making submissions have pointed out the particularly harsh impact of legislation of this nature on the gay and lesbian community in Canada. We have seen the extent to which Canada Customs has been prepared to single out periodicals directed to the gay and lesbian community and many of the bookstores which service that community. L'Androgyne bookstore in Montreal, the Glad Day bookstore in Toronto, and Little Sisters in Vancouver all have had to fight debilitating and expensive court battles merely to obtain the right to distribute materials which in no way fall into the category of abusive, violent or degrading materials. Under this legislation, it is quite likely that similar materials would come under attack as well.
One of the concerns that has been raised by the periodical marketers of Canada is that this legislation will still leave unclear exactly what is and what is not subject to criminal sanction. They point out that there are many areas of the legislation that are confusing and unclear, leaving responsible marketers in the position of being unable to determine whether action would be brought against them for handling certain material.
The bottom line on this legislation is that it falls far short of what we as New Democrats have called for, which is strong and effective legislation to deal with violence, with degradation and with exploitation, and to deal with the sexual exploitation of children. That is not the scope of this Bill.
The scope of this Bill indeed would go well beyond that, as has been pointed out by Pierre Berton and many others who
Criminal Code
have had an opportunity to examine the legislation. Indeed, the Toronto Public Library Board, the largest library system in Canada, has indicated that it is so outraged over the provisions of the Bill that it plans to shut all of its libraries in protest for one afternoon early next month. As the chief librarian states: "It is a move to try to publicize our concern about this very bad law, but it is also to give us a chance to have a public meeting to explain the implications to both staff and the public".
Considering the failure of this Bill to respond in a serious way to the concerns of the country, to respond to the kinds of recommendations that were made by the Fraser Commission and to make the fundamental distinction between erotica and pornography, I move:
That the motion be amended by deleting all the words after the word 'that' and substituting the following therefor:
"This House declines to give second reading to Bill C-54 because it fails to clearly define pornography as material that condones violence, coercion, abuse and degradation in its depiction of human beings or portrays or promotes the sexual exploitation of children; and also, because it does not distinguish pornography from material of an artistic, literary, educational or scientific nature in a fashion acceptable to the Canadian public, including artists".
I have consulted with the Chair as to the procedural acceptability of the amendment. I understand that it is indeed within the scope that is allowed in the area of reasoned amendments.
In conclusion, I want to repeat what I said last Thursday, that if this legislation is adopted it will make Canada the most culturally repressive nation of all of the western democracies. It is an attempt to pander to the extreme right wing of the Conservative caucus. It is legislation which fundamentally violates the provisions of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms in Canada in terms of freedom of expression. It fails to make the distinction between imagery which portrays sexuality and imagery which portrays violence, degradation and sexual exploitation of children.
It is a fundamental step backward for Canadian society and I hope the House will adopt the amendment which I proposed and tell the Government to go back to the drawing board and bring before the House legislation which reflects the true concerns of Canadians and does not reflect the very narrow concerns of the moral majority element in Canadian society.

speakeroldname: Mr. Richard Grise (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, of course we will be giving very serious consideration to the amendment to Bill C-54, because indeed we must now debate the NDP amendment motion which reads as follows:
That the motion be amended by deleting all the words after the word "that" and substituting the following therefor: "This House declines to give second reading to Bill C-54 because it fails to clearly define pornography as material that condones violence, coersion, abuse and degradation in its depiction of human beings or portrays or promotes the sexual exploitation of children; and also, because it does not distinguish pornography from material of an artistic, literary, educational or scientific nature in a fashion acceptable to the Canadian public, including artists".
Madam Speaker, when the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) introduced his motion he may have forgotten that there has been a parliamentary reform since the Conservative Government was sworn to office in 1984, and I would suggest his motion is completely out of order. As I see it, the first thing to do is to accept the Bill as drafted and refer it to a legislative committee, as was the intent of the parliamentary reform and as was the wish of the three political Parties when it was
decided to change parliamentary procedure so that as many Members as possible would be able to express their views and be party to the decision-making process. Madam Speaker, I suspect the purpose of parliamenraty reform was not to promote filibustering even before a bill has gone through second reading, even before the Opposition Parties have had an opportunity to debate it.
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to take part in the debate on Bill C-54 designed to amend the Criminal Code with respect to pornography. I believe that all individuals interested in Bill C-54 ought to take time to study Criminal Code section 159 concerning obscenity. Although many private citizens and groups have criticized Bill C-54, they do not seem to understand the present law in Canada. Many correspondents have qualified our existing obscenity laws as vague and lacking in guidance. A publication is deemed to be obscene if its dominant characteristic is the undue exploitation of sex. It also mentions sex connected with violence and cruelty, among other things.
What is undue exploitation? The courts have tried to define this expression on the basis of community standards. Obviously, our penal code should be as clear and specific as possible so that citizens will know what acts are criminal and what the penalty is for this behaviour. Bill C-54 proposes a specific definition of child pornography, degrading pornography and pornography involving criminal acts or violence.
Madam Speaker, Bill C-54 must reflect the concern of all Canadians for putting an end to the alarming escalation of the availability of violent, degrading and increasingly explicit pornographic material, as well as material depicting child pornography. Hon. Members are aware that at the present time, our Criminal Code prohibits the production, publication, and distribution, and the possession for those purposes of any obscene material, written or otherwise. A publication is deemed to be obscene if its dominant characteristic is the undue exploitation of sex or of sex and any one or more of the following subjects, namely crime, horror, cruelty and violence. The Canadian courts have adopted a test reflecting "common moral standards", to determine what should be considered undue exploitation, based on what the Canadian public as a whole is prepared to tolerate.
Judgments handed down by Canadian courts have shown that the present provisions of the Criminal Code dealing with obscenity are difficult to apply. The result is a lot of confusion and concern among the public, retail merchants and distributors, and also among the police, Crown attorneys, counsel for the defence and judges. The present uncertainty about the law and how it is to be interpreted has helped to modify the character of pornography today and expand its market. In recent years we have seen a disturbing increase in the availability of pornographic material. In addition, the format in which such material is available has also become increasingly varied: video recordings, films and satellite telecasts have been added to the traditional media such as books and magazines.
November 30, 1987

All this material is now available in an increasing number of stores and boutiques.
The public has expressed its concern about the use of children in pornographic material and about the availability of this kind of material to young people.
We are all aware of the excellent work done by the Special Committee on Pornography and Prostitution, chaired by Mr. Paul Fraser. In its report tabled in the Flouse of Commons in April 1985, the Special Committee recommended a complete review of the Criminal Code's provisions on obscenity.
This Government has held extensive consultations across the country with groups of experts, and the public has made it very clear it expects the Government to adopt appropriate legislation to deal with the problem of pornography.
Madam Speaker, in my view, the aim of Bill C-54 is to provide a solution to this problem. The Bill provides a clear and precise definition of pornography and erotica, something no previous legislation has done. The new definitions will make it easier for the courts and the public to determine what kind of sexual material may not be produced or distributed.
The Bill creates a new offence, that of dealing in pornographic material, with penalties depending on the nature of the material. In addition to visual matter depicting child pornography, violent sexual behaviour and sexually degrading acts, the definition of pornographic material includes everything that encourages or advocates such activities.
However, Bill C-54 also tries to strike a balance, since it is not solely concerned with creating new offences. In fact, it provides for new defences by excepting pornographic and erotic material used for educational, scientific and medical purposes or having artistic merit. I may point out to those who are so hysterical in their criticism of this Bill that these defences are an improvement, since they are not explicitly provided in the present legislation.
Madam Speaker, I would now like to comment on what was said by the Hon. Members for Outremont (Mrs. Pepin) and Burnaby (Mr. Robinson). It was suggested that the Bill would not only allow the Government to interfere with what goes on in the bedrooms of the nation, as the Hon. Member for Outremont remarked, but also with this country's museums and art galleries.
In my opinion, these remarks were entirely ill-disposed. First of all, Madam Speaker, the Bill does not deal in any way with the sexual behaviour of people or what Canadians do in the privacy of their bedrooms. Even a most superficial interpretation of this Bill would lead us to this conclusion. As far as museums and art galleries are concerned, it is true that the Bill makes it an offense to display erotica in a way that is visible to a member of the public in a public place, unless the public must, in order to see such erotica, pass a prominent warning notice advising of the nature of the display. However, when there is such a prominent warning notice, there is no offense.
Criminal Code
It should be emphasized that this Bill provides for a defense based on the fact that the erotica has artistic merit or an educational, scientific or medical purpose. If the accused, therefore, can establish that erotica has artistic merit or an educational, scientific or medical purpose, the Court will have to find him non guilty.
It has been suggested that the literature on AIDS and other sexually transmissible diseases is so explicit that it could be forbidden. This again is a remark which ignores the defences provided for in this Bill and which are based on its scientific or medical purpose.
Some have also criticize the Bill because of its very wide scope, including visual representations of sexually explicits scenes between consenting adults. I must be clear on this point. The Government had no intention of amending the Criminal Code concerning the explicit representations of sexual relations.
This type of representations is already considered as obscene under Section 159 of the Criminal Code. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) has referred to the R.C. Video World Limited case, where the Supreme Court of Canada confirmed a ruling by the Appeal Court of Manitoba to the effect that the depiction of vaginal, anal or oral sexual acts, as well as masturbation were obscene. In my opinion, Bill C-54 does not amend the gist of that ruling.
Some have felt that the Bill is much too tough on those renting pornographic material involving children, suggesting that they should be liable to lighter penalties then the producer of such material. In my opinion, we should not yield to this type of reasoning. Child pornography is certainly what we find most awful and most repulsive. The producer, the distributor and the renter of this type of material are guilty of a most criminal act and none of them should be punished less severely than the others.
Madam Speaker, the purpose of this Bill is to make the fight against pornography more efficient and to give the necessary precision to the law.
Madam Speaker, I come back to the motion of the Hon. Member for Burnaby asking that Bill C-54 not be read for the second time. In his own statement and in that of the Hon. Member for Outremont (Mrs. Pepin), we find that it is extremely important and even essential to do everything possible to eliminate child pornography and to remove violence from erotic or sexual material.
Now, once more, Madam Speaker, we are faced with what, since parliamentary reform, could nearly be an unparliamentary amendment, as we are discussing a Bill and we have mechanisms such as the Legislative Committees to propose amendments-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I in no way questioned the ruling of the Chair. A while ago, Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier rose on a point of order to say that the Hon. Member for Burnaby had tabled certain papers in both official languages and he blamed the Government for not doing the same thing regularly. For the information of the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier), Madam Speaker, I should like to emphasize that his comment was not referring to an amendment when a Minister had tabled a document, but simply a matter of information and a document to be laid on the Table.
Madam Speaker, I should like to deal once more with the highlights of this Bill on pornography which guarantees the freedom of expression as provided for in the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, while defining a limited category of materials which will be forbidden because of their pornographic nature.
The Bill reinforces and clarifies current legislation on obscenity through new provisions on pornographic material and erotica. It clearly defines the forbidden pornographic material. First of all, any visual matter that shows children or young people involved in sexual activity, extreme violence in a sexual context, sexually violent conduct, degrading acts in a sexual context, bestiality, incest or necrophilia, as well as explicit sexual behaviours.
Also, any matter or commercial communication that incites, promotes, encourages or advocates any conduct which I have just mentioned. These definitions of forbidden material take into account the current legislations dealing with obscene material which reflect our social standards.
The Bill proposes a new offense, in the case of a person who deals in pornography and who is involved in making, importing, selling or renting pornographic material. Such a person is liable to various penalties depending on the nature of the pornographic material. Every person who possesses pornographic material involving children is guilty of an offense punishable on summary conviction.
The Bill provides for special defences based on the artistic merit of the material or its educational, scientific or medical purpose. The accused will not be able to use these special defenses in the case of the most baneful pornographic material involving children or violent acts in a sexual context.
Whenever the defender successfully uses the artistic merit of a document as a defense, the Court will declare that such document is not pornographic. Erotica include explicit depiction in a sexual context or for the purpose of sexual stimulation of the viewer, of certain parts of the human body. Erotic material can be displayed behind a barrier showing warning about the nature of the material, or it can be covered by an opaque wrapper, and it must not be sold or rented to young people. Performances with children or youths and involving sexual acts or any pornographic representations are prohibited. Under the provisions on hate propaganda, the groups which can be distinguished by sex will now be protected against hate pornography, which will be an offence under the customs tariffs, as will be the importing into Canada of pornographic material.
Madam Speaker, the Government consulted several groups when preparing Bill C-54. I asked myself serious questions earlier when I heard the Hon. Member for Burnaby say that librarian groups, for instance, object to this Bill because they will have to reorganize certain documents, books and publications in certain areas of their library. What should be the most important in our society today? Not to change anything, or to impose certain standards and restrictions to our librarians to protect our young people and teenagers when they go to the library, and we know that an increasing number of young people go to the libraries, which is certainly a good thing! Is it not normal to want to keep such material away from our young people and to require that there be a special section in libraries for erotica which will not be acessible to young Canadians? I believe that this is much more important.
Then, there is the issue of access to certain types of publications and films for young people under 18 in the stores. For instance, there are many video stores where young people can take out movies themselves with their video club member cards. It is now quite easy for young people to rent cassettes depicting bestiality, violence and sexual acts between youngsters. It is important to remove access to such products from our youths.
Madam Speaker, it has also been suggested that Bill C-54 will prevent our medical researchers from developing products against AIDS and other sexually transmitted diseases. Making that kind of comments is totally absurd, as if medical progress
November 30, 1987

would be at a standstill if pornography could not be used as a tool. That is what the Opposition Parties have been saying. Plow can anyone imagine that in 1987, if medical science were deprived of pornography, no progress will be made to fight against sexually transmitted diseases!
Madam Speaker, nor do I think-
That is not what was said.

I am about to conclude, Madam Speaker. With respect to sexual education, today we have a training or educational system which enables our children-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: But it is not by allowing ready access to pornography that we will improve the sexual education of our children. It is obvious that with the proposed amendment, and this will be my last comment of course, we are against the proposed amendment. I would urge Hon. Members to adopt Bill C-54 as quickly as possible and refer it to a legislative committee so as to give better protection to the Canadian population with respect to sexuality, child pornography and pornographic violence.

Madam Speaker, I would like to make some comments and conclude with a question. I think my Conservative colleague is to some extent misrepresenting the purpose of a Bill that is supposed to deal with pornography. The words pornography and sexual conduct are now mentioned in the same sentence, so it is very easy to say that people are in favour of violence and pornography, while completely neglecting to mention that, since sexual conduct is mentioned in the same sentence, all kinds of sexual conduct and erotica are prohibited.
The Hon. Member said earlier that Opposition Members were hysterical in their criticism of the Fraser Report. I think he knows perfectly well this Bill does not in any way reflect the Fraser Report's recommendations. I invite him to read the Fraser Report and the speech I made in the House last Thursday, in which I referred specifically to the Fraser Report.
Women's groups that are campaigning against pornography and violence have condemned this Bill, their comment being that it was all black and white. And regarding what my Conservative colleague said about doctors and that it was ridiculous to expect works of art or colour slides that were not pornographic to be confiscated, I gave him an example of an incident that occurred in Calgary, in October 1987, when three RCMP officers confiscated forty-two slides belonging to a women's coalition group that was giving presentations to demonstrate what violence was, the dangers of pornography
Criminal Code
and the difference between pornography and erotica. The RCMP officers confiscated the lot and said: You are doing a pornographic presentation.
So we protest. And since the police will be defining what is art, what is medical and what is pornography, then this Bill will have to be rewritten because the way it is worded now, you are making no distinctions at all.
In concluding, I would like to ask the Hon. Member a question. As it stands now, the Bill criminalizes sex. Read your definition of pornography and tell me why you want to include something that is not criminal. Today, a sexual act is not criminal, and you want to make it a crime in this Bill. Explain the difference between pornography and sex and why you want to criminalize a sexual act?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, first I should like to point out to the Hon. Member for Outremont (Mrs. Pepin) that women's groups are not opposed to the Bill itself, they are against certain definitions. They want explanations and more information, but they are not directly against the Bill. So there is a slight difference between the comments of the Hon. Member for Outremont and what the various women's groups are saying about the Bill.
Madam Speaker, I should also like to refer to this Bill in light of the existing legislation about which the Hon. Member for York Centre, I believe, said:
"Taken with our proposal on sexual violence and degradation, we think this provision of the present Criminal Code is worth preserving".

When we read the text of the Hon. Member for Outremont (Mrs. Pepin) who is saying that the existing legislation should be repealed altogether ... In the Bill we are saying that that part of the Bill will be kept, as a result of the Supreme Court ruling concerning the Manitoba court. The Hon. Member for Outremont is saying that anything in Bill C-54 which relates to what is already in the existing legislation should be deleted.
So with respect to pornography and sexuality I think that Bill C-54 specifies quite clearly what we are deleting, what we are trying to prevent in pornography, and we are not by any means undermining the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms as far as sexuality is concerned.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to take this opportunity to commend the Hon. Member for his contribution and for recalling certain facts dealt with in this legislation with respect to the definition of pornography.
Madam Speaker, I have as a woman, for years, of course, in private and public life, been fighting with other people and making representations to all levels of government in the hope that one of them might stand up and do something to stop the

November 30, 1987
Criminal Code
degradation of women and children. And, finally, Madam Speaker, I can now proudly claim 1 am part of a government that has the political courage to push matters one step further.
I would like to suggest to the Hon. Member that, as we must remember, as far back as 1978 the previous Government has attempted ... It is easy for the Hon. Member for Outremont to speak from the other side of the House, because when they were on this side, Madam Speaker, as the situation was getting worse, as public patience was running out-because there was so much degrading material, it had come to the point where children were actually murdered for the sake of having films getting more pornographic, and closer to real life. It is easy to suggest from the Opposition benches that the legislation does not address the issue.
Madam Speaker, when the Leaders took their stand during the 1984 elections, they clearly stated they were going to do something. We came up with Bill C-54 and we of course deal with the definition.
Madam Speaker, I for one know when something is erotic and when it is pornographic. And it is my view that the justices of the Supreme Court, the judges of the lower courts, know when something is erotic and when it is pornographic. It is written down in the Bill. My view is they are playing party politics, which is really out of place here. For partisan reasons, they come up with fiddlesticks in order to suggest that the Bill is bad, that we should throw it away! Come now, that is absolutely ridiculous!
I would like to suggest to the Hon. Member for Chambly that women in my view agree with this Bill. They had one reservation as to the definition, but I think that if they read Bill C-54 carefully, they will realize it is clear and precise as to what is erotica and what is pornography.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to thank my colleague the Hon. Member for Argenteuil-Papineau and Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mrs. Bourgault) for these very relevant clarifications. Indeed we must stop playing partisan politics with such an important measure concerning child pornography. As Members of the House holding a mandate from the population, how can we tell the Government: Your Bill is no good, scrap it and go back to square one! How can we do that? Madam Speaker, for too long already we have been letting people condone violence through the youth pornography trade.
Madam Speaker, again I repeat, it is unbelievable that a motion be introduced to reject the Bill. They are giving short shrift to this measure, supposedly because their Party has no use for it. It does not matter whether Canadians want it or not. Opposition Members on the other side have decided there is no rush, not to worry, we can afford to put off dealing with child pornography and pornographic violence for six months, a year or even longer. And we as Government are supposed to accept that!
I conclude, Madam Speaker. As my colleague the Hon. Member for Argenteuil-Papineau pointed out, what women's groups want-and I think they are directly involved in this issue, when we talk about pornography, a legislative measure on pornography-they have shown quite clearly that they do have reservations about some of the definitions, but at no time did they ever object to the principle of the Bill.

Madam Speaker, as a Member of Parliament and as a very active feminist, I am very concerned that we get good pornography legislation; so I am supporting an amendment which I think will take us somewhere in that direction.
We want tough legislation, but it must be carefully drafted. It must distinguish very clearly between what we want to ban- that is, violent, degrading, coercive pornography and child pornography-and what may be objectionable to some people but on which there is not a great deal of consent within Canadian society that it is at the level of being pornography to be banned. We must make it very clear. We might want to have some restrictions on this kind of material, for example, that it not be freely available everywhere where it would offend people and that it not be available to children. We must have very, very tough laws on pornography.
I think Bill C-54 is an attempt to go in the right direction. At least I give the Government credit for wanting to bring in tough and careful legislation, but unfortunately it makes a lot of mistakes. However, they are mistakes which can be redressed. Definitions can be redrafted. Careful work can be done. We could sit down with experts, with representatives of the women's movement, with representatives of the churches, and with representatives of art groups, to come up with something that would have broad Canadian acceptance. I am quite confident of that, but we do not quite have it in the Bill before us. We do not have it yet. It could be done at committee, but there must be agreement on the part of the Government to make real amendments.
Let me make very clear that my Party wants tough legislation. I want to read into the record a resolution that was passed at an NDP federal convention which is absolutely crystal clear in terms of the kind of legislation we want. It reads:
WHEREAS women's groups throughout Canada are deeply concerned about the avalanche of pornographic material which condones violence, coercion, abuse and degradation in its depiction of women and children;
WHEREAS such images are demeaning and destructive in their effect on the social fabric of Canada; and
WHEREAS there is growing evidence of a causal link between such pornographic material and the increase in violence towards women and children,
THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED that the federal New Democratic Party:
November 30, 1987

1)	defines as pornography material which condones violence, coercion, abuse and degradation in its depiction of human beings and condemns the production and distribution of such material whether in film, video, print, or any other form;
2)	condemns the production and distribution of material which portrays or promotes the sexual exploitation of children and calls for severe penalties for offenders;
3)	calls for a strengthening of Section 159 of the Criminal Code of Canada to reflect these concerns;
4)	calls for amendments to the Broadcasting Act to prohibit the broadcasting of such pornographic material, with severe penalties for violation including the possibility of revocation of licence;
5)	calls for amendments to Section 281 of the Criminal Code of Canada to add sex as a prohibited category, and to strengthen the penalties and provide a clear method of enforcement under this section so that pornographic material which degrades the human person can be prosecuted as hate literature;
6)	calls on the New Democratic Party to participate in actions across Canada to develop public opposition to pornography as a form of hate propaganda, and to seek solutions to the problem.
That is tough, that is what we want, and I hope we will get it.
I want to commend the many people who worked on this issue. I particularly want to thank Mrs. Ulma Lee and Korean Christians in Toronto who have worked very diligently to bring forward petitions with literally thousands of names to protest pornography and to ask for a strong Bill C-54. I think the work was excellent. I was pleased to see it, and I fully support it.
Where will we go from here? We have proposals from many people, groups, experts, and so forth asking for careful redefinition. I should like to refer to a brief from the United Church of Canada, a very large church within society. It wants tough legislation. It wants amendments to the Bill. It commends the Government for bringing it in, but it asks the Government to work on amendments. The brief reads:
Bill C-54 distinguishes between erotica and pornography in terms of degree of explicit activity.
It asks for the qualitative, not the quantitative, difference to be taken adequately into account. It continues:
We believe the difference between erotica and pornography is a matter of quality of relationship rather than mere quantity of activity or inactivity.
We submit that the difference between unhealthy pornography and erotica cannot be measured in degrees of explicitness, but rather is determined in terms of context. Explicit sexuality in a context of commitment, mutuality, free choice, and non-violence is a good gift of God.
Pornography, in contrast, is the depiction of sexuality cut off from its full human context. Pornography loses sight of the whole person, focusing only on his/her ability to sexually gratify.
Women are reduced to vagina and breasts and men to the size of their genitals ... By portraying human persons, usually women, as sexual playthings eager to respond instantly to male, female, sexual demands, human persons, usually women, are turned into sexual objects, degraded and robbed of their humanity.
I think that is all too true. The United Church asks for amendments to take into account, in a very careful way, what these differences are. The church shows where it supports the Bill and where it needs to be amended.
Criminal Code
There is an extensive Bill from the committee against pornography which documents the way the courts have been dealing with the existing legislation. It goes to show the liberalization in our society and the growing acceptance of pornography as it becomes more and more available and harder and harder to fight. It shows also how the definition proposed in Bill C-54 is inadequate in both directions, namely, it includes some material which the vast majority of Canadians would not want included.
There are many ways in which Bill C-54 itself is not tough enough. There are loopholes that would allow some material to go through as erotica which most of us in a common sense approach would say is thoroughly offensive, degrading and humiliating normally to women and children. We need to have amendments in both directions. It shows, for example, a wrinkle which I had not thought of where the visual image may not be pornographic in and of itself but, with the text, the impression conveyed is one which is thoroughly degrading, humiliating and invites violence and degradation toward women and children. We have to take into account the whole effect. The present wording, by focusing on a dominant part of the image, may be very, very pornographic in its intent and result, although what makes it so may not be dominant in the quantity of the portrayal. Here we have a loophole.
There are pages of recommendations for careful amendment, but I cannot go into them in detail here. We need to pay attention to them. I hope the Government will look very carefully at the recommendations of this organization and that people will be active at the committee stage working for good amendments.
The question of the arts and pornography is a very difficult one. We have had representations from many arts organizations. They are afraid they will go into jail, that individual artists will be prosecuted, or they will have to censor themselves out of fear of prosecution. Artists, with very few exceptions, do not have very much money. They will have to hire lawyers to protect themselves. Clearly we need to have a law which does not include in pornography artistic, scientific, literary, educational work and documentaries. That is not the intent of the Government, but we have to make very clear that that intent is adequately reflected in the legislation, and I do not think it has yet been done adequately. The Canadian Association of University Teachers has proposed over the years amendments to ensure that that is the case. I think the Government has attempted to respond, but it has not done well enough so far.
Unfortunately, some artists are not helping by saying they do not want to have any pornography legislation whatever, that their creative spirit should be allowed to have full play without any law interfering with what they want to do. I do not believe artists ought to be above the law, and I would invite them to sit down with legislators and experts to see that we get a law that is fair. We do not want to prosecute artists. We

November 30, 1987
Criminal Code
want to distinguish between what is largely the pornography business, the billion dollar business coming from the United States, mass produced and schlock from California, which is what this Bill is all about, and artistic and literary works. This is what the women's movement is addressing when they say they want tough legislation on pornography, but we do not want to cast the net so wide that we include artistic and literary works.
Artists have to work and be constructive in proposing amendments. It is not good enough to say that they want nothing whatever.
I recall being lobbied by an artist who said he did not want to see any limits at all on his freedom of expression. I asked him about the extreme case of snuff movies where someone is actually killed in a pornographic setting, normally a woman. He said there should be a classification of films, to which he would agree. That kind of film would get a classification of a double X or a snuff movie classification, but he added that there ought to be no prosecution of the artists involved. The person committing the murder could be sought for murder, but the film would be shown. This would be a work of art and people would analyse it and deal with it as a work of art, a film in which somebody is actually killed, which is preposterous. I am shocked to hear this sort of proposal and to hear that actors and directors would ignore the violence taking place in order to pursue artistic endeavours.
Artists have to ensure that there are limits on pornography leading to violence against women and children, women being forced to re-enact pornographic scenes in magazines, videos and so forth and children being abused in more imaginative ways. Artists are sensitive members of society, but they are members of society with responsibilities to their neighbours. They have to have it on their conscience that violence against women and children is something to which we must put an end.
What about the hate literature aspects? This Bill would include sex as one of the categories for prosecution, and pornography is included here. That is desirable, and the New Democratic Party resolution to which I have referred also specifies that. However, our resolution goes much further and says it must be made applicable. Right now the hate literature sections of the Criminal Code are virtually unenforceable, so that merely putting in the word "sex" is entirely a political endeavour. It is something that will not have any practicality in making it possible to prosecute. By all means add sex to that list, but make that section enforceable, otherwise it is only window dressing and hardly good enough for the real problems.
We need to get experts and people from women's organizations to sit down and constructively work out something better. There is no doubt that the pornography issue has been a difficult one for the women's movement. After all, women have a very wide variety of concerns, expertise and interest, and political views go from one extreme to the other as to what
should be included and excluded in the Bill. There is a strong body of opinion in the women's movement to have tough laws, but they must be carefully nuanced. We have major organizations-not just extreme organizations-for example, the United Church, which asked for precise amendments, and we must look at those.
Let me raise one difficulty which comes from the United Church brief. Erotica, the sexual explicitness which is not coercive, which is consensual between adults-which does not include or involve abuse or exploitation of a child-is desirable and good. Yes, in principle, obviously it is so. If a man and a woman want to make home movies of their sexual activities, why not? Whose business is it apart from their own? However, once you get into commercial exploitation, on stage, film, television or video, you have a different set of problems. It is not so easy to deal with the question once you get into hiring someone to take on these roles.
How would you portray a consensual relationship between an adult man and a woman within a relationship? The United Church and other groups say that so long as there is consent and it is part of a relationship, it is not a degrading act, one person acting on another. Sexuality is part of human relationships and it is good to show that. Yet how do you do it in a film? Are you going to show the people as married? Are you only going to allow actors and actresses married to each other or who have a long-term relationship with each other to perform in these roles? The sex act can result in procreation. Do we really want children to be conceived in an act done for commercial purposes?
We are not just talking about ordinary events, we are talking about something that is qualitatively very different. I do not think people have looked at those aspects, it is all very well to say, yes, this is a healthy relationship and there is no reason why it should not be portrayed. However, once you get into hiring people to perform these roles, then you get into really serious problems, such as sexually-transmitted diseases. Should an actor or actress get a sexually-transmitted disease, including AIDS, as a result of taking on one of these roles?
There are a lot of questions which have not been adequately gone into. Experts have to sit down and consider these questions. They have to get out of this land of principle and high position which says that we are in favour of this because it is consensual, not exploitative. How is it going to be realized in a practical sense when actors and actresses, directors and so forth, are engaged professionally to perform roles of this sort? That is a much more difficult question.
I do not have very much time left so I want to conclude by suggesting that we need to have the Bill withdrawn, hold consultations with experts, and do some serious redrafting. Or, if the Government uses its majority to pass this Bill at second reading, it should go into committee and the various concerned
November 30, 1987

groups and experts should be invited to work on redrafting it at that stage.
I want to assure members of the Government that my Party will support the Bill at third reading if we get a good Bill back, and there are reasonable amendments which take into account the kinds of criticism we have raised. We want a practical response to a real problem. We have been waiting for this Bill for a very long time. We had the Fraser Commission back in 1984 and Badgley dealt with child sexual abuse before that. We really want to get moving on this.
The Government will have our full support, as I said, if it deals very carefully with this legislation. I hope this is not just a political gesture where the Government will be able to say it tried to get a pornography law through, but the Opposition would not let it. I hope it is not just a public relations effort to appeal to a certain amount of political opinion. It should be a serious endeavour to address a serious problem affecting the life and health of women and children in particular, and the dignity of everyone. I hope we will have serious amendments so we will be able to put in place a law which responds to the real situation where we have a lot of pornography, a lot of degradation, and in which women and children for the most part are suffering as a result. Let us get on with that task.

Madam Speaker, I want to express appreciation for the Hon. Member's speech. I always listen to her with great interest and usually with great benefit. I was very encouraged by the support she gave for the principle of the Bill and the Government's initiative in introducing it in this House. However, all of that led me to wonder why she would support her Party's amendment to the Bill. What she wants in the way of a further careful review is surely possible at committee stage. Why else do we have a committee stage? Why prejudge it? Why assume that we are not going to have a serious assessment of the legislation by a committee which will include members of her own Party? When she urges a careful review, she is not simply urging it on members of the Government but also on members of her own Party.
In view of the reasoning contained in the Hon. Member's speech I wonder why we need the amendment? This is especially true in light of her conclusion, which was that we have waited a long time for this Bill. We are certainly going to wait a long time because it will need careful examination in committee. Therefore, why does she want us to wait longer still by supporting this amendment? If it passes, and I trust it will not, it will simply cause extended and, I have to say, futile delay.

Madam Speaker, I suggested in my remarks that there are two possible ways of proceeding. One is for the Government to withdraw the Bill and redraft it right now. The Government could agree to do that and, in an informal and speedy manner, work on redrafting. The other possibility is to have the Bill go to committee. At that stage it could redraft it.
Criminal Code
The reason for the amendment is to propose the speedier way of working. Redrafting can be done more efficiently in a more informal setting. Committees take time to meet. Their meetings depend upon the schedule of Members of Parliament, what happens during the Christmas holidays and other break periods. Committees meet only three days a week at most. If this were turned back to the Government for redrafting, the work could begin today. Consultations could take place on an all-day basis. One could assign people to work on the Bill without having to follow the sometimes cumbersome formalities of a committee.
I think we might be able to work more expeditiously by withdrawing and redrafting, but I certainly assure the Hon. Member that if the Bill is passed at second reading, we will work on it in committee. It may take a bit longer and be a bit more cumbersome, but we will certainly work constructively in committee if that is the way the Government chooses to go.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I agree with my colleague for Scarborough West (Mr. Stackhouse) that the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald) has, in all her time in this House, always shown her concern about the problems related to child pornography, the degradation of women, and so on. Madam Speaker, as for young people today, about two weeks ago, I was invited to the CEGEP de TOutaouais where the students had organized a discussion similar to those on the program Parler pour parler with Janette Bertrand. The students invited me to play my own role of Member of Parliament. The subject being discussed was pornography and the pornographic material available everywhere. From what they said, the situation seems very clear to young people. They pointed out that some young Canadians have said that there should be specialized stores for purchasing pornographic or erotic material as exist in the United States and in other countries.
They say that when they see movies showing acts of violence, if there has not been that much open discussion in their own families, they are traumatized by this type of material. They believe that the Government was right to introduce Bill C-54. The Hon. Member says that it would be easy for the Government to withdraw this Bill and to rewrite it, but she knows quite well that it is not that easy in Parliament. As pointed out by my colleague for Scarborough West, why does the Hon. Member not ask her colleague for Burnaby to withdraw his amendment and to tell the House Leaders: Refer this Bill to committee as quickly as possible because there will be representations by the groups concerned about the definition. Everyone knows that it is not easy to define sexual issues. It is an extremely complex subject. Why does the Hon. Member not suggest that to the House immediately? It would be more logical and quicker. We could adopt the Bill and put an end to the degradation of women and children.

November 30, 1987
Criminal Code

Madam Speaker, with regard to speed, we have been waiting a long time for this. This is the third year of the Government's mandate, and I think it could have proceeded very much more quickly. We have had the Badgley and Fraser reports for some time. The Government has been very slow to act. I have explained why I think that objective could be best achieved by redrafting.
The difficulty is that if we pass a Bill which contains a lot of mistakes we will be in a lot of trouble. There will be charter cases. The law which exists right now is very bad and is not very enforceable. The courts are starting to chip away at it because it does not have adequate support. If this Bill is passed without significant amendment there will be a lot of objections. People will fight it. The courts have gone in a very liberalizing direction. They have been allowing more and more pornography. You cannot enforce a law which people do not support. There must be tightening up in that area.
It is also true that there are some loopholes. The violent and degrading pornography which we are against is not included. Therefore, the law errs in both directions. In some respects it is too lenient and in other respects it is not lenient enough. This Bill needs very careful redrafting or we will be in a lot of trouble. We have a lousy law on the books. Let us take the time to ensure that we have a good law on the books which will be enforceable.

Madam Speaker, I was interested in the remarks of the Hon. Member with regard to national women's organizations. I wonder whether she would elaborate on some of the concerns which have been raised by these groups. At its last annual general meeting it adopted a resolution that the NAC reject the proposed legislation on pornography and lobby the Government to ensure that any new legislation focus on violence rather than sexual acts, not affect the distribution of sex education material to people under 18, and not reinforce heterosexualism, and that the NAC lobby the Government to ensure that any legislation puts the onus on the Crown to prove that material does not have artistic merit rather than, as is the case now, putting the onus on the artist to prove this, which is very likely in breach of the provisions of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
The Hon. Member is a former President of the NAC. Perhaps she could elaborate on some of the concerns which have been raised by respected national organizations, such as the National Action Committee for the Status of Women, with regard to this legislation.

Madam Speaker, the National Action Committee is Canada's largest such organization. It is an umbrella organization which includes groups from the extremely conservative to the extremely unconservative. There is, therefore, a division of opinion within NAC itself on how to proceed. There is certainly near unanimity on having tough
laws. Concerns have been raised as to bias in the laws and the onus on artists to defend themselves. I think there would be a great deal of support for that.
I keep in touch with NAC executive members. They are keen to have a well-worded Bill passed. They are prepared to appear before the committee. Their position may be a little like mine. I believe that there are two routes to follow. The Bill could be withdrawn and redrafted. However, if the Bill goes to committee, they will be there to suggest practical and constructive amendments. We can certainly count on their support and expertise in achieving the objective of having a very carefully drafted Bill on pornography.

Madam Speaker, I was prepared to speak on Bill C-54 and welcomed the opportunity to do that. However, I understand that in the last few minutes an amendment has been moved that we not now give second reading to this Bill. I strongly disagree with the mover of that motion and with his reasons for it.
1 would like to confine my remarks mainly to why we should proceed with Bill C-54. I believe that this Bill is a guide for the future use of the Canadian public. Guidelines have to be set by Parliament. Therefore, it behooves every Member in this Chamber to accept the responsibility which we have been elected to perform, that is, to help set those guidelines.
Both the Fraser and the Badgely reports clearly pointed out the magnitude of the problem of pornography and child abuse in our society today. Upon reading these reports one must open one's eyes and recognize that even in what we like to think of as "civilized" societies atrocities are occurring to children and families, atrocities which can be tied to the availability of hard and soft core pornography.
The committee examining the sexual offences against children, commonly referred to as the Badgely Committee, found that there are two main sources of child pornography in Canada; importation and private individual production. The Fraser Commission concluded that 85 per cent of all pornographic material in Canada comes from the U.S., 12 per cent from Europe, and 3 per cent is made up domestically. Whatever the source, the people of Fraser Valley East and, undoubtedly, many other areas of Canada, want pornography stopped. Pornography offends our standards and demeans, degrades and abuses the persons involved.
Even the word "pornography" incites an emotion, the scope of which depends on the outlook of the person using it. I tend to believe that if Canadians knew the degree to which pornography was available, or in fact what pornography is, each and every one of us would stand up and shout, "We are not going to take it any more".
Bill C-54 has some very positive points. For the first time a definition of pornography will be added to the Criminal Code. The definition is clearly written in the Bill, so I will not get into it at this time. However, we are clearly cracking down on child pornography and violent behaviour. I am pleased to see
November 30, 1987

that other Members of this House do agree with that part of the Bill.
I strongly support the Bill as it now stands but would like to see it go even further. Specifically, 1 believe that there are too many ways out by proving artistic merit or educational, scientific or medical purpose. This leaves too much to interpretation. If the courts are to determine in each case whether a piece of work has artistic merit, we need to know the parameters for this term. It seems obvious that one person's idea of what is artistic is not another person's. "Artistic merit" will become the gateway for pornographic material to enter Canada and be circulated. This could become a major flaw in the Bill.
There are theories which suggest that a direct causal link exists between violent pornography and violence against women, although others state that this connection is somewhat difficult to prove. The Fraser Commission report concluded, albeit reluctantly, that available research is of limited use in demonstrating that pornography is linked to the causing of actual physical harm, but it strongly submitted that there is definite harm associated with much of what is pornography.
Arthur Gary Bishop, convicted of sexually abusing and killing five young boys in the U.S., once stated:
If pornography material would have been unavailable to me in my early states, it is most probable that my sexual activities would not have escalated to the degree they did.
He further stated that pornography's impact on him was devastating and "was a determining factor in my downfall". I find this statement absolutely frightening.
The final report of the Attorney General's commission on pornography, published in the United States in 1986, serves to show us that there are acts that need to be seen not only as the cause of immorality but as manifestations of it. Even though it may be difficult to find a causal link between pornography and violence or abuse, this report makes a very good attempt. It is well worth reading.
Let me briefly outline the highlights of the chapter entitled "The Question of Harm". Two categories of harm are identified. The primary category of harm is not where the act leads, but simply what it is, such as murder, rape and assault. The second category deals not with what the act is, but where it will lead. We can fit pornography into this category.
Even though no cause is exclusive, the report states that pornography is harmful because it causes some people to commit acts of sexual violence, because it:
causes promiscuity, because it encourages sexual relations outside of marriage and because it promotes so-called unnatural sexual practices which lead men to treat women as solely existing for the sexual satisfaction of men.
There may never be conclusive proof that a causal connection exists, if "conclusive" means that no other possibility exists. However, the Attorney General's Commission on
Criminal Code
Pornography states that there are multiple causes, that is, if they were to identify one cause and eliminate it, while having all the other factors remain the same, the problem would at least be lessened.
This is a very important point. Why must we wait for empirical evidence to point out one causal link between pornography and violence? Instead, it is time to acknowledge that if we correct the causes we have identified we will at least help alleviate the problem.
My constituents believe that the link I have been discussing does exist. Pornography not only causes physical harm in many cases, it causes social harm in all instances.
In today's fast-paced world, it is difficult enough to raise and protect our children. When we must constantly be on the look-out for negative external influences, the battle is even more uphill. More and more school boards are integrating a program for teaching our children to say no in an effort to prevent child sexual abuse. This is a sad statement on the way our society is heading.
Could we not prevent a lot of this abuse of our children by working hard to stop those who make or import pornography? Bill C-54 will be a start, a framework, from which I hope we can continue to take a stand against pornography, particularly as it relates to children.
The 1984 Badgley report stated that child pornography is a direct product of child sexual abuse. It states: "It comes into existence, and can only come into existence, through the base and coldly premeditated exploitation of a young person's sexual vulnerability". This is very clear. It is not the children who should or can be blamed because they are but the tools used by exploitative individuals for their own end.
The report states further that: "Where a young person has been used in the making of visual pornographic material, it is irrelevant whether some view the material as having literary, artistic, or aesthetic value". The point is that it is permanent abuse of the children and perpetuates the warped idea that children are available for such purposes.
We must also worry about the availability of pornographic material to our children. Municipalities can only regulate the pornographic industry by the way they determine how such material can be displayed.
This fall referendums were held in some of the municipal elections in Fraser Valley. Citizens clearly pointed out their abhorrence of pornography. I am proud of the stance that they took on this important issue.
It is difficult to decide what is pornography and what is artistic merit. The U.S. Attorney General's Commission on Pornography attempts to separate pornography into four levels or categories. The first and most serious is sexually violent material. This type of pornography features actual or unmistakable simulated or unmistakably threatened violence presented in sexually explicit fashion. Conclusions from
