Criminal Code
clinical and experimental research clearly indicate an increase in the likelihood of aggressive behaviour toward women as a result of exposure to this type of material.
This is not to say that everyone watching this type of pornography will become violent, but let me remind the House of Arthur Gary Bishop, the murderer whom I quoted earlier. It is not surprising that the images that people are exposed to bear a causal relationship to their behaviour.
The second level or category of pornography is non-violent material depicting degradation, domination, subordination or humiliation. This type of material bears some causal relationship to attitudinal changes. For example, rape will be viewed as less serious and the victim as more responsible. We may become somewhat numb to the reality of the crime.
The third level or category is non-violent and non-degrading materials in which the participants appear to be fully willing participants. These activities affect our perception of promiscuity. Therefore, the ultimate harmfulness of much of this type of pornography reflects individual views. This type was found to be particularly harmful when it fell into the hands of children because this is not the way that children should be taught about normal sexual relationships. This type of pornography separates sex from love, commitment and marriage, and it is that effect that is negative.
The final category of pornography as defined in the U.S. Attorney General's report is nudity. This raises the problem of trying to establish when nudity stops being mere nudity and begins to have sexual undertones. Most of us would not find certain types of nudity harmful, such as that meant plainly for educational purposes, but certainly we must agree that nudity in other cases, and in the wrong hands, can be harmful. This brings us back to the question of what pornography can do to our children.
The Badgley report gave some startling statistics with regard to the access of children to pornographic material. It found that 540 different pornographic magazines were being sold in Canada and that six of seven retail outlets surveyed displayed these well within the reach of young children. Clause 159.7 of Bill C-54 states:
Every person who displays any erotica in a way that is visible to a member of the public in a public place . . . must (in order to see the erotica) pass a prominent warning notice advising of the nature of the display therein or unless the erotica is hidden by a barrier or is covered by an opaque wrapper, is guilty of an offence punishable on summary conviction.
This is a welcome amendment, but is tempered by the next clause which gives the accused a way out, that being artistic merit or educational, scientific or medical purpose. Again, this is too subjective.
Bill C-54 also includes an amendment to the Customs Tariff Act by adding pornography as defined in this Bill to the list of items not allowed for importation. Since over 80 per cent of all pornographic materials come from the United States, tightening our laws may help prevent some material from coming into Canada. I only hope that this goes far enough.
I realize that there are many responsible groups who believe that this Bill is not definitive enough, and that even some libraries are stating the opinion that some of the material they have for educational purposes could be interpreted as pornography. However, I believe that this Bill goes a long way in helping us to get to the root of the problem.
Finally, I would like to compliment the Government for the Bill as it has now been initiated to try to curb pornography. By helping to curtail the openness of pornographic material, Bill C-54 will have a positive influence on the family, and any laws the Government makes are to be used as guides for society. I can assure the House that this Bill will receive my support. I would urge all other Hon. Members to vote against the amendment before us and to support the Bill as it now reads.

Madam Speaker, I would like to ask my hon. friend whether or not he finds there is some displacement with respect to concerns around this Bill, for instance, the description of erotica and erotic material versus pornography and pornographic material? I can well appreciate that we have a need for this kind of Bill which will address the concerns of violence and pornographic material and its impact on men, women and children. However, I fail to understand the section on erotica. I also fail to understand not only the definition of erotica but the clause which deals with the display of erotica and exhibition of erotica to persons under 18.
Does the Hon. Member plan to take his children or his nieces and nephews to the museums of our country to show them the creative arts our artists see and which we display and enjoy? If so, what does he plan to do with some of the very beautiful nudes which are presently on the walls of our museums? How does he expect to handle that particular aspect of the Bill?

Madam Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for her question. Yes, I have taken my family to these museums and have found the artistic merit and composition of the art forms indeed very enlightening, but I think the Hon. Member is missing the point of what we are trying to accomplish in the Bill. We are trying to get at the publications and advertising, trying to set some guidelines and standards for what we will accept to be displayed in the open market. While 1 firmly believe that when parents take their children to museums to see art it is a good thing and it is the right thing, by the same token, I believe there must at least be an attempt on the part of the Government to get at a very crucial issue. I am happy to see that the Hon. Member does acknowledge the fact there is a problem in our society with which we have to come to grips. This is only an attempt to come to grips with the problem.
If we can improve this Bill in committee when going through the clause by clause study, I am sure Hon. Members will welcome that. But I come back to my original premise, that this is a start, it is an attempt to try to correct something that
November 30, 1987

is very harmful to our society. I am sure the Hon. Member agrees that this has to be done.

Madam Speaker, I would like to ask the Hon. Member a question with respect to the kinds of imagery to which he has referred which would in fact be illegal under the provisions of this legislation. The Hon. Member has said he does not want in any way to tolerate imagery that might promote promiscuity. However, does the Hon. Member not recognize that the approach which the Government is taking, and which the Hon. Member seems to be taking, judging from his remarks, is a very dangerous and dictatorial approach? While his own personal standards may be those which he has outlined in the House today, and he is certainly entitled to those standards, what he is suggesting is that the police should enforce his conception of morality on all other Canadians, and if his perception of what should be allowed to be seen is somehow different from other people's perception, even if they are in the minority, they should be subject to criminal sanction. That kind of heavy-handed Victorian approach to sexuality is surely dangerous in Canada today.
Why would the Hon. Member make illegal, as would the Hon. Member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan) who has just entered the Chamber, this kind of imagery? Why would he subject those who wish to have images of adult consensual activity not involving any violence or degradation, why would he make the distribution of that kind of material, a subject of criminal sanction?

Madam Speaker, I do disagree with the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) as to what should be the guidelines for our society. It is the responsibility of this House to talk in terms of what are our freedoms and responsibilities. Too often in a very free society we have to come down so far on the side of freedom that we fail to assume the responsibility for the harmful nature and effect of certain things on our society.
While we can talk in terms of what consenting adults will do, nonetheless we do not have to have it in explicit form displayed on the shelves of our newsstands and put into our theatres. I see this as a start at getting at that very harmful influence on our society.
If the Hon. Member would be perfectly honest, he would agree that there have been harmful effects to our society from the hard-core pornographic material that is out there on our bookshelves nowadays, and at long last we must come to grips with this.

Madam Speaker, I want to congratulate my colleague on his remarks and say that I wholeheartedly support action taken now rather than a delay on this matter which is so crucial to society. I also want to pass along compliments to the Hon. Member for Broadview- Greenwood (Ms. McDonald) for a very thoughtful address. She said in her remarks that the New Democratic Party will
vote on third reading, in any event, for a Bill to curb pornography. Therefore, I would ask the Hon. Member, in view of the comments made by the Hon. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone) and the question just asked by the Hon. Member for Burnaby, if those are not precisely the kinds of questions that should be asked in committee, which is the reason parliamentary committees are set up? Why should we even consider a nonsensical amendment to withdraw this Bill when everyone in this Chamber agrees it is high time we got around to dealing with this critical issue of pornography? Why should we agree with the amendment? Why would Hon. Members not agree right now to send this Bill to committee where it belongs?

Madam Speaker, I think the Hon. Member for Hamilton-Wentworth (Mr. Scott) brings up a very valid point. He was even better at expressing that point than myself. 1 want to re-emphasize that it really behooves Hon. Members to set the guidelines. We are the ones who are responsible. That is what the law is all about. It is the guidelines for the type of society we want to live under and be part of. While I uphold freedom in the truest sense of the word, nonetheless I want to take the responsible action we must. Therefore, I wholeheartedly say that we have to defeat the amendment put forward by the Hon. Member for Burnaby and pass the Bill.

subsubtopic: HELP FOR VICTIMS OF CRIME-REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT CONTINUE PROGRAM TO ASSIST VICTIMS OF VIOLENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, millions of dollars are spent every year on rehabilitation programs and mental health services for criminals. Victims of violent crimes, however, suffer long term mental problems as a result of these violent acts. It seems terribly unfair that criminals should receive mental health services while their victims must be personnaly responsible for the expenses of the psychiatric help they need.
The Department of National Health and Welfare has just cancelled its "Victims of violence" program which was established in 1984 with a view of getting a greater understanding of the mental health problems of these victims. I

November 30, 1987
wonder what the Government is prepared to do for these victims and why it has abolished this modest but useful program.
Mr. Speaker, I hope the Government will realize that although it is important to provide our criminals with psychiatric help, it is even more important to help the victims of these crimes. I ask the Government to reimplement as soon as possible its assistance program.

subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT FLOW THROUGH SHARE RATE REMAIN THE SAME FOR NEXT THREE YEARS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the tax reform will be upon us very soon and we are well aware that the flow through share scheme has not been abolished. But the people living in Abitibi, Temiscamingue and other Quebec mining areas want to make sure that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson)'s tax reform goes in the right direction, insisting that now is not the time for reducing the 133 1/3 rate of the flow through shares.
Faced with free trade, it is vital to protect investment capital formation in the mining industry.
Mr. Speaker, Quebec prospectors and businessmen, the mayors of Abitibi and Temiscamingue, the elected representatives of these ridings in the House of Commons, and especially the whole population want this 133 1/3 rate to remain the same for the next three years.
Now, in the Abitibi-Temiscamingue region, the unemployment rate is 7,4 per cent, down from the 24 per cent and 27 per cent it was previously. Private industry has often been a very good partner in our region's economic recovery. Today, the junior members of the mining sector deserve this support from the Government of Canada for the next three years.

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF MANAGED PRICE SYSTEM IN BRITAIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the federal-provincial conference of First Ministers, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and Premier Grant Devine indicated that any economy that gave up free trade for some form of managed prices was doomed to failure. Yet consider the experience of Margaret Thatcher's Britain where changing
from a free trade grain market to high domestic prices under the managed pricing of the European Economic Community resulted in unprecedent rural prosperity in Britain.
How can the Prime Minister and the Premier explain the great leap forward rural Britain has made under the common agriculture policy? Was that rapid progress not the result of going to $8 per bushel wheat instead of buying cheap imports? Was the rejection of the cheap food policy not the chief engine of growth for rural Britain?
Given the obvious success of the British experience in abandoning free trade for agriculture, why are Conservatives here forcing this option on the people of rural Canada?

Mr. Speaker, on Friday a day-long dialogue took place in this institution between parliamentarians and the science and engineering community. It was organized by COPSE, the Committee of Parliamentarians, Scientists and Engineers, and the Royal Society, and was intended to bring parliamentarians up to date on an array of current social and economic issues with scientific overtones.
The symposium started with a remarkable presentation by the Speaker of this House in which he outlined how important it is for parliamentarians to be familiar with modern science because of its importance in the solution of many pressing global problems.
Some of the topics discussed included Canada's changing population, new developments in material science, global change, the impact of science on the North, space technology, the AIDS epidemic, bio-technology, the environment and sustainable development. The symposium ended with a creative presentation by John Polanyi, Nobel Laureate, on the importance of basic science and its eventual linkage to the market-place.
Parliamentarians who participated found the day remarkably informative, and we want to thank you, Mr. Speaker, and COPSE and the Royal Society for your and their contribution and support of a positive, historic, and creative day. It is dramatically important that parliamentarians like myself become more aware not only of the importance of research and development but of the manner in which it can be used to solve in a political way the very complex problems with which society is confronted.

November 30, 1987

subsubtopic: ALBERTA-DECISION ON USE OF FRENCH IN LEGISLATURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the decision by Premier Getty to ban the use of French in the Alberta Legislature, without prior approval, is more than regrettable. It is a shameful betrayal of Canada's policy of official bilingualism.
Moreover, in light of the recent Meech Lake Accord, it serves to depict the Premier's weak and unacceptable definition of bilingualism.

To him, official bilingualism is but a Quebec regional policy. His endorsing of the "distinct society" clause was very convenient for him because it enabled him to play Pontius Pilate to Alberta's 60,000 Francophones. He should at least recognize French as a working language in the legislature, otherwise his signing of the Meech Lake Agreement was but a hypocritical charade. Mr. Getty should not hesitate to immediately reverse that shameful and ill-advised decision.

subsubtopic: CENTRAL AMERICA-REPORT ON VISIT BY PARLIAMENTARIANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week a Canadian delegation visited Central America in the cause of peace.
As part of that delegation I was privileged and happy to meet hundreds of Canadians who have been working for humanity in that region for many years. Typical of them is Joseph Gunn of the riding of Scarborough West who has been serving the Save the Children Organization.
Some of them have been there for a complete career, such as Bishop Corriveau and many of his clergy in south Honduras. Others have made a recent career change, for example, two Salvation Army captains who conduct a clinic for treating alcoholics and drug addicts in the city of San Jose, Costa Rica.
Whatever be their work, whatever be their background, they are still Canadian citizens who value their citizenship and remember their country with happiness and gratitude. I speak of them today in order that they can know Canada remembers them and that they are honoured within its Parliament.

subsubtopic: STATUS OF FRENCH IN PROVINCIAL LEGISLATURES-RESPECT FOR LINGUISTIC DUALITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as M.P. for the Canadian constituency with the largest number of French-speaking people outside Quebec, I greatly deplore the decision made by the Alberta Legislative Assembly to treat French as any other language except English. In my view, it does not make sense to require that a French-speaking Member, in any province in this country, beg permission from someone else in order to speak in his mother tongue at the Legislative Assembly.
Mr. Speaker, I myself had the privilege and honour to serve as M.P.P. in a province where the use of French was not officially recognized, but at least in the Province of Ontario we had the right and privilege to speak in French if we so desired at the Legislative Assembly, although there was no simultaneous translation. I urge Alberta's Premier to reconsider that decision made in his Assembly recently and I also urge the Canadian Government, whose responsibility it is to look after official languages in Canada, to take a stand on that most important matter for all Canadians and to uphold this country's linguistic duality.

subsubtopic: TRIBUTE TO CANADIAN ORDER OF THE AMERICAN HELLENIC EDUCATIONAL PROGRESSIVE ASSOCIATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this evening the Canadian Order of the American Hellenic Educational Progressive Association is hosting a special banquet to honour the hard work and dedication of Canadian parliamentarians. However, I wish to commend AHEPA for its dedication to the assimilation and education of Greeks within their country of immigration.
AHEPA was formed 65 years ago. It is a philanthropic, socially conscious organization which not only operates within its original mandate but also participates in the broader social, political, and civic life of its community.
The AHEPA family of Ottawa has honoured Dr. Wilbert Keon for his remarkable achievement with heart transplants, and Dr. George Mintsioulis for his equally remarkable ability to restore sight with precision eye surgery.
The Ontario Special Olympics were singled out for special recognition since they produce real winners and give mentally handicapped individuals a true sense of their self-worth.
All Canadians can be proud of the contributions made by the Canadian Order of AHEPA, for its promotion of tolerance

November 30, 1987
and co-operation, and for its dedication and commitment to build a better Canada.

Mr. Speaker, democracy in Haiti lies a bloody tattered corpse, struck by many mortal blows delivered with impunity as the governing National Council averted its eyes from the horror precipitated by its own refusal to act.
To those who have observed the tragedy of Haiti as it has unfolded there can be no doubt that the governing National Council has engineered a coup for which it had long prepared. Once again a brutal military with easy access to modern arms has used them to brutalize its own people.
Canada and other Governments should act now to signal their utter and complete rejection of the junta, and explore within the Council of the United Nations how nations of the world may effectively intervene to give democracy another chance in Haiti.
Canada should oppose any unilateral intervention which will inevitably replant the seeds of colonialism which lie at the roots of Haiti's tragic history.

subsubtopic: INACCURATE PORTRAYAL OF THE LATE BILLY BISHOP, V.C.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canadians are by now aware of the deliberate negligence displayed by the National Film Board of Canada when it produced and released "The Kid Who Couldn't Miss", the wildly inaccurate portrayal and betrayal of Billy Bishop, holder of the Victoria Cross, and the most decorated Canadian serviceman ever.
I ask the Minister of Communications (Miss MacDonald) to join me in opposition to Ms. Joan Penefather, the vice-film commissar of the National Film Board and the currently the leading critic of Billy Bishop, and request from the Chairman of the National Film Board the immediate removal from circulation of the film "The Kid Who Couldn't Miss", which really should have been called "The Film That Missed Badly". Thank you, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate my friends of the New Democratic Party in Quebec who, as a result of their excellent weekend convention in Montreal, have shown that the NDP now has strong roots in Quebec. In three years, NDP-Quebec membership went up from a few supporters to nearly 8,000. Associations have been established in 90 provincial counties and two thirds of Quebec's federal ridings. Some 360 delegates attended one of the best NDP convention I have ever seen.
There can be no doubt that the NDP will rally sociodemocratic supporters and that it is becoming the real voice of most Quebecers, men and women alike, at both the federal and provincial levels, while remaining an autonomous provincial Party.
I congratulate Mr. Rolland Morin for having been elected leader of the NDP-Quebec, and I expect that in the very near future we will see true NDP Members from Quebec in the Parliament of Canada and in the National Assembly of Quebec.

Mr. Speaker, for the first time in history I believe we have a Government which is expressing firm leadership in placing agriculture on the top of the priority list.
As recently announced under the Grain Stabilization Program, all member farmers will receive their final payment by early December. Approximately $1.4 billion has been committed for the 1986-87 crop year. Saskatchewan alone will receive $377 million, bringing the level of assistance under the program up to $759 million this year in our province.
As well, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has assured farmers that a deficiency payment will be made before Christmas to assist farmers who, through no fault of their own, are in an extreme cost-price squeeze.
In addition to current assistance for farmers, the Government is working at providing a long-term solution for eliminating subsidies at the international level. Our Government worked very hard to place agriculture on the agenda for discussion at the new round of GATT talks in Uruguay and at the Venice and Tokyo Summits.
November 30, 1987

Long gone are the Trudeau days under which the then Prime Minister asked farmers in Saskatchewan: "Why should I sell your wheat?"

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the question is relevant: Where is the solidarity? What about the Meech Lake Accord? What about the commitment of the provinces to maintain both official languages?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what happened to the Meech Lake spirit? What happened to all these provincial undertakings to preserve the duality of Canada? subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS ALLEGED TAPING OF MANITOBA PREMIER'S CONVERSATIONS

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS ALLEGED TAPING OF MANITOBA PREMIER'S CONVERSATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister.
Will he explain what one of his officials was doing taping the private conversations of Howard Pawley, Premier of Manitoba, during the First Ministers' Conference? Does this practice conform with the Prime Minister's theory of ethics in government?

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS ALLEGED TAPING OF MANITOBA PREMIER'S CONVERSATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, no one from the FPRO from the federal Government was taping anybody's private conversations.
What takes place at the First Ministers' Conference is a continuation of FPRO practices that have gone on in the past. Simply when Premiers, during the course of scrums, are giving public comments a representative of the federal Government is there, only in regard to public comments, to bring to the attention of the federal Government the extent to which these comments might impact on the ongoing federal-provincial conference. All of these were done publicly and pursuant to past practice.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS ALLEGED TAPING OF MANITOBA PREMIER'S CONVERSATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have checked with the previous administration and that practice was not followed.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS ALLEGED TAPING OF MANITOBA PREMIER'S CONVERSATIONS
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS ALLEGED TAPING OF MANITOBA PREMIER'S CONVERSATIONS
speechtext: Hon. Members laugh. It is symptomatic of how they view the public conduct of business in this country.

subtopic: QUERY CONCERNING INSTRUCTIONS GIVEN TO OFFICIAL DOING TAPE RECORDING

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: QUERY CONCERNING INSTRUCTIONS GIVEN TO OFFICIAL DOING TAPE RECORDING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Premier Pawley is reported to have said that the taping took place not only of scrums but of private conversations and informal receptions.
On September 20, 1985, in this House when the Prime Minister was confronted with a leaked government communications strategy relating to the trade negotiations with the

November 30, 1987
Oral Questions
United States, suggesting a campaign of dirty tricks against opponents of the deal, including the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry, myself as the Member for Vancouver Quadra, and the Member of Parliament for Saint-Henri- Westmount, the Prime Minister gave us his assurance that that practice would not be followed. I quote what he said:
I give that assurance-because we stand for individual rights and liberties.
Why then was a public servant taping Premier Pawley's private conversations? Who instructed the official to tape Premier Pawley's conversations? Was Premier Pawley singled out, or were other Premiers having their conversations taped at the same time? What kind of sneaky, sleazy operation is the Prime Minister running in this country?

subtopic: QUERY CONCERNING INSTRUCTIONS GIVEN TO OFFICIAL DOING TAPE RECORDING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are running the same kind of operation that was in full force pursuant to directives of the previous Liberal Government in 1978 and 1982. I am informed that a similar process was in place at the 1978 and 1982 First Ministers' Conferences on the economy and the 1981 constitutional conference.
Information officers of the FPRO were assigned to record public comments, at scrums, made by Premiers which related to the agenda of the First Ministers' Conference. That is all that was done and it was quite proper and pursuant to practices of previous Governments. If my right hon. friend has any information at variance with that, please share it with the House.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have checked previous practice and it does not accord with what the Prime Minister is saying. The Premier of Manitoba said his conversations were being taped not only at scrums but in private conversations at cocktail parties and informal receptions, and he was being shadowed and tailed throughout the conference.
Oh, oh!

I ask the Prime Minister how often this practice has occurred? Is it an official dictum of his Government that First Ministers should be surveyed, taped and followed while at First Ministers' Conferences? I would also ask if it is his policy to tape only those Premiers who oppose the trade deal, and are those of us opposed to the trade deal supposed to be engaged in subversive activities?

No, Mr. Speaker. The private conversations at cocktail parties and this kind of stuff that my right hon. friend seems to have some knowledge of- perhaps he could share the specifics with the House. The information I received from the FPRO indicates exactly what I have told the House. No one was shadowed or tailed. In fact I suspect that if anyone in this country was
going to be shadowed or tailed, Mr. Pawley would be among the last.

subsubtopic: HAITI-CANCELLATION OF GENERAL ELECTION-REQUEST FOR SUSPENSION OF CANADIAN AID
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Secretary of State. I think he will share the incredible sense of disgust and reprehension most Canadians felt over the spectacle in Haiti this weekend involving the squashing of the first light of democracy and the reinstitution of government by torture and intimidation that we witnessed on our television screens.
In the Government's official response to the Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade Committee's report on foreign aid, the Government says that where violations of human rights are systematic, gross and continuous, government to government aid is denied or reduced. The basic principle is to ensure that repressive regimes are not legitimized through Canadian development policy.
Considering that the situation in Haiti clearly violates the standards set out in that statement, is the Government prepared either to suspend or reduce government to government aid to Haiti until such time as the innocent people of that country can return to the polls without being threatened by death squads running loose in that country, as they were this weekend?

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Landry (Minister for External Relations):
speakerposition: Minister for External Relations; Minister responsible for La Francophonie
subsubtopic: HAITI-CANCELLATION OF GENERAL ELECTION-REQUEST FOR SUSPENSION OF CANADIAN AID
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to inform the Hon. Member that of course the Government was shocked, and disappointed when it first heard about yesterday's events in Haiti.
I must say, however, that our aid program is very specifically directed to the neediest groups in Haiti and that at this moment, we do not think it would be appropriate to withdraw from these people, who really need Canada's help, their very means of survival.
I can assure Hon. Members that our aid to Haiti does not go directly to the government. It is not a blank cheque for the government. Generally speaking, it always goes through nongovernmental organizations and provides some support for institutions, in order to help the people to help themselves.

Mr. Speaker, I will address my supplementary question to the
November 30, 1987

Secretary of State for External Affairs. His colleague says that the Government will not do anything about aid, but the question clearly is what the Government is going to do in terms of a statement or action on behalf of Canadian people against this regime.
I would like to remind the Minister of clearly stated government policy. Where there have been repression and a denial of rights, there has been a clear and unmistakable contradiction of these principles.
Will the Government not take action commensurate with those standards to show that this country will not stand by and allow democratic rights to be snuffed out and that kind of intimidation to continue?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we stated the policy which the Hon. Member quoted. We are, as my colleague said, shocked and deeply disappointed by the developments in Haiti and particularly, as she indicated outside the House, by the questions relating to the role of the Government of Haiti itself in these developments.
We do not have all the information which we require in hand. The Government and the House would certainly not want actions taken by Canada to disrupt the flow of aid to those people who are most needy which would, consequently, impose a double hardship upon them.
However, if it is clear that the authorities in Haiti have been contributing to the disruption and destruction which we saw yesterday, as may very well be the case, the policy which was referred to by my colleague and which was stated by the Government in response to the standing committee will be followed. I think the House would share our desire to ensure that we have all the relevant information in hand before we take action of that kind.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-REQUEST THAT GENERAL ELECTION BE HELD
CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-REQUEST THAT GENERAL ELECTION BE HELD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister knows that the Government of Canada did not have a mandate to negotiate a free trade deal arising from the election of September, 1984. It is now too late to have one before the proposed date of signing on January 2.
In an interview on the weekend the Prime Minister seemed to rule out having an election before January 1, 1989. The Prime Minister knows that complex legislation has to be passed by the Parliament of Canada, by the provinces of Canada, by Congress, and by many States in order to implement such an agreement some time during the course of 1988.
Oral Questions
Does the Prime Minister not think that the most responsible thing to do, both in terms of getting a democratic mandate and in terms of being conducive to good Canada-U.S. relationships, is for the Government of Canada to have an election sometime early in 1988 so that the people of Canada will have an occasion to demonstrate their views on this important matter?

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-REQUEST THAT GENERAL ELECTION BE HELD
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Government has a mandate to engage in and provide economic renewal for Canadians. Within three years we have created a million new jobs. I think that is exactly what the Canadian people want.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-REQUEST THAT GENERAL ELECTION BE HELD
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-REQUEST THAT GENERAL ELECTION BE HELD
speechtext:
Economic renewal finds expression in many changing and challenging ways. One of them is to innovate, to be daring, and to provide leadership in the world of new trade, new technologies, and new economic prospects and possibilities for all Canadians.
Pursuant to the creation of a million new jobs in three years this is exactly what we have done. We hope to be able to do this on a regular basis. At an appropriate time the Canadian people will have an opportunity to express their views.
Mr. Speaker, many Canadians would think that to be daring, innovative, and responsible would be to get a mandate from the people of Canada before acting.
Hear, hear!

I would like the Prime Minister to consider the serious implications for Canada-U.S. relations of proceeding in 1988 without an election. At this time he has the support of only five of the provinces. Three provinces are opposed and two are undecided. Both opposition Parties in the House of Commons are against.
Does the Prime Minister not think that the responsible thing to do in terms of his obligations to the people of Canada and the implications for Canada-U.S. relations in the future, is to go to the people of Canada in 1988 with his message and let them decide between him on the one side and those of us on the other?
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian people know that both opposition Parties are against. They are waiting to find out what you are for.
Hear, hear!

Call an election and you will find out.

November 30, 1987
Oral Questions

With regard to our obligation to provide for economic renewal, my hon. friend seems to discount very quickly the creation of one million new jobs within the space of 37 months. The first 10 months of this year have brought about the creation of some 375,000 new jobs, which is a very important record.
My hon. friend will be interested in the quality of these jobs. Ninety per cent of the jobs created are full-time as opposed to part-time job creation, and 55 per cent of these one million new jobs have gone to women. That is economic renewal at its best, and we plan to continue this program of economic renewal.

I would even add that when the Prime Minister began the negotiations we had a $20 billion surplus. We have about a $7 billion surplus now. If the Canadian economy is so strong, why is the Government rushing headlong into one of the most complicated deals in Canadian history? That is the issue that has to be faced.

If the Prime Minister wants to make his decisions as a man who supports democratic principles, why does he want to deny Canadians the right to say yes or no to the proposed trade agreement with United States? Why not make this a democratic decision?

Mr. Speaker, there will be a democratic decision at the appropriate time. If I am not mistaken, the Canadian Constitution gives us a five-year mandate, and it is up to the Government to act responsibly during that time. There is also parliamentary tradition, and we still have one year to go before we finish our fourth year. We still have to deal with some important issues. I think that what we have achieved today should be reassuring for my hon. friend. If he is at all serious, and I know he is, he must be very happy with an almost unique job-creation record, more than one million new jobs, with the job-creation rate in Quebec seven times what it was under the previous Government. That is good news for Canada and Quebec. At the appropriate time, Canadians and Quebecers will have a chance to express their opinion, and I am sure the Hon. Member will regret the outcome!

work by reason of the lockout. Thousands of Canadians are deprived of services. subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-POSITION OF FORMER U.S. RESERVE BOARD OFFICIAL

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Paul Volcker, former head of the U.S. Reserve Board, in his keynote address last night to the fortieth anniversary of GATT in Geneva said that while he had to support any new trading arrangement between Canada and the United States, he went on to warn: "Trade deals, such as the Canada-U.S. deal, are a threat to the system of multinational trade and could degenerate into regional trading blocs". What is the response of the Prime Minister to these statements? Does he not feel that such

November 30, 1987
Oral Questions
criticisms delivered to almost 100 nations in the world can do irreparable damage to Canada's stature in the eyes of our international trading partners, both present and future?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-POSITION OF FORMER U.S. RESERVE BOARD OFFICIAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the negotiations into which we have entered with the United States are explicitly authorized by the GATT and are entirely consistent with the GATT. More than that, other trading nations in the world know as we do of the force and destructiveness of protectionist pressures in the United States.
I have spoken, if the Hon. Member has not, to Trade Ministers and Foreign Ministers of other countries, all of whom welcome this initiative, both because it demonstrates to the protectionists in the United States that there is a way to deal in the world other than hiding behind walls, and because it is breaking new ground that will be important to the whole GATT in terms of the new issues that have been dealt with in the negotiation between Canada and the United States and that can serve as a model for the world, establishing trading rules in matters like services, investment, and other fields where there are not now good enough rules.

Mr. Speaker, in response to the seemingly endless criticisms and weaknesses of this trade agreement, the Prime Minister on the weekend had one soothing, sweeping, cleansing message. He said: "Don't worry, it will all come out in the wash". False!

And, by the way, where is the final text? When will it be released? It will all come out in the wash all right, after Canada has been put through the wringer and hung out to dry. The only wash the Prime Minister knows about is a whitewash.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Transport, the Hon. Member for St. John's West, is absent today so my hon. friend will have to await perhaps a direct answer.
Meanwhile, the Hon. Member refers to the weaknesses of the free trade agreement. If that is so, this will come as a great surprise to countries such as Korea, Taiwan, Japan and Israel, all of which, having been apprised of the realities of the Canada-U.S. trade agreement, want to negotiate a similar agreement for themselves because they think it is such a fine trading instrument.

subtopic: UNITED STATES OFFER TO SELL SUBSIDIZED GRAIN TO U.S.S.R.
UNITED STATES OFFER TO SELL SUBSIDIZED GRAIN TO U.S.S.R.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
Oral Questions
On Friday the United States offered the Soviet Union another highly subsidized sale of grain. That is the third offer this year from the United States to the Soviet Union, and the second since the signing of the trade deal with our Prime Minister and President Reagan.
In light of the fact that a few weeks ago in the House the Secretary of State said that this was at least a violation of the spirit of the trade agreement and that he would talk to Mr. Shultz in Brussels, I wish to know now from the Secretary of State for External Affairs why the Government is so ineffective, incompetent, and inept, that despite talking to Mr. Shultz on Friday of last week, the United States made another offer to the Soviet Union, which is an important market for Canadian grain, using a subsidy that violates the very deal signed by the Prime Minister and the President of the United States?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: UNITED STATES OFFER TO SELL SUBSIDIZED GRAIN TO U.S.S.R.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just to be precise, and I know that the Hon. Member would wish to be precise, what I said and what I believe is that this is inconsistent with the spirit of the deal. I do believe it is inconsistent with the spirit of the deal. I think it makes bad sense in trade law, and I think it makes bad sense in terms of promoting the acceptability of the trade arrangement that has been negotiated between Canada and the United States. I do not think it serves the interests of Canadian or American farmers, but it is part of the trade war in agriculture that is going on between the European Community and the Government of the United States. We are victims of that war.
As was indicated in a statement made by a Member of this House earlier this afternoon, we have been among the leaders in the establishment and functioning of the Cairns Group to try to bring an end to that type of costly conflict between two massive Treasuries.
No one regrets more than I do that the United States is carrying on that type of program. So far, the reality is that, despite those programs, the quality of the production and reputation of Canada have meant that we have been able to maintain and even increase our share of world markets, but that does not make what the United States is doing acceptable.

I mentioned the offer of last Friday, but according to the press today China has accepted to buy some 265,000 tonnes of wheat under the U.S. Export Enhancement Program of subsidies.
What on earth is George Shultz telling the Secretary of State for External Affairs? Why are we so ineffective at putting the message of Canada across when it is a direct violation of one of the sections of this trade deal that the Prime Minister wants to sign with President Reagan? Why are we so ineffective?

Mr. Speaker, what he is telling me is that the Export

Enhancement Program is not a policy that the United States administration mounted, nor one that it likes, but is part of the law of that country. Particularly in the circumstances of an election year, I am afraid that we will face more of those types of actions under the Export Enhancement Program.

subsubtopic: QUALITY AND SPEED OF TRANSLATION SERVICES-RULING OF MR. SPEAKER
speechtext:
I should like to advise Hon. Members that I have a question of privilege and a point of order upon which to report to the House.
On September 22, 1987, the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Epp) raised a question in relation to the Translation services required by Members of Parliament. A point of order of a similar nature was also raised on November 18, 1987 by the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin). The Chair has carefully considered both matters and, because of their similarity, will deal with both of them in the ruling.

The Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon referred specifically to two occasions when, to put it in his own words, "the translation services of the House of Commons and of the committees of the House have been hard pressed to fulfill their obligations, and to enable Members of Parliament to complete their work and carry out their duties".
In the first instance, the Hon. Member argued last spring that the work of the Standing Committee on Multiculturalism was impeded because the translation of documents was not always available at the time the committee was considering various drafts of a report. In the second case, the Hon. Member referred to the one week delay in the presentation to the House of the report of the Special Joint Committee on the 1987 Constitutional Accord because of difficulties encountered in completing the Translation work. The Hon. Member suggested that the problems facing the Translation Bureau are the direct result of staff reduction in recent years and the policy of contracting out translation work since 1978.

In his contribution on the issue, the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) most appropriately reminded the House that, when requiring translation services, the House of Commons is merely a client of a Government department, namely the Department of the Secretary of State. The Chair also appreciates the good words of the Hon. Member regarding the exceptional quality of the translation provided by the Translation Bureau, despite the recurrent difficulties.
The Hon. Member for Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme) was right in talking about the sensitivity of the whole issue and the frustrations felt by some Members when unable to benefit from the necessary services in order to function adequately in their own language.
Point of Order

Last November 18, the Hon. Member for Regina West apprised the House of the fact that two meetings of the Standing Committee on Transport had to be cancelled because its report, sent to the Translation Bureau three weeks earlier, had not been translated. The Chair had this matter investigated and it was discovered that the Translation Bureau had negotiated with the research branch of the Library of Parliament, which is preparing the report, an extension of its deadline to complete the translation. This was done without the committee's knowledge. Although this is clearly an administrative misunderstanding, and not a point of order, it nevertheless shows again how the operations of the various committees of the House can be frustrated.
In relation to the question of privilege raised by the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon, the Chair would like to indicate at the outset that, in order to establish that there exists a prima facie case of privilege, the Speaker must be satisfied both that privilege appears to be sufficiently involved to justify giving the matter precedence over all other matters before the House, and also that the matter is being raised at the earliest opportunity, as specified in Citation 81(1) of Beauchesne's Fifth Edition.
While considering the matter, the Chair consulted the precedent of November 5, 1968, to which the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon referred in his intervention. At the time an Hon. Member complained about the insufficient number of translators and interpreters available to meet the needs of the House and its committees. Speaker Lamoureux did not find a prima facie case of privilege, but acknowledged the merits of the Member's grievance.
The Chair cannot conclude otherwise in the present matter raised by the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon. Neither the House nor the Members were prevented from actually performing their duties, although I would admit that access to some of the working tools was not made easy for some Members. Therefore, the Chair must find that the matter raised by the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon does not constitute a prima facie case of privilege.
But, as was the case with Speaker Lamoureux in 1968, the Chair finds the matter of the utmost importance and is thankful to both the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon and the Member for Regina West for raising it in the House. It is, indeed, very distressing to realize that some Members and, in particular, francophone Members, do not have the same immediate and ready access to documents and files as other Members have. It creates an unfairness which is simply not acceptable.

As indicated by the Hon. Member for Saint-Denis, the Chair has been very sensitive to this issue. While one understands the problems facing the Translation Bureau in the management of its operations, the House, as a special client, is

November 30, 1987
Criminal Code
right to express its concerns to the Department of the Secretary of State with respect to translation delays. The Board of Internal Economy has examined the matter in the past and officials of the House have approached the Translation Bureau on many occasions in order to improve the situation and to see that the level of service provided fulfilled the best expectations of the House of Commons.
We were assured by the Department of the Secretary of State, last April, that every effort would be made to avoid delays, but in the light of the comments of Hon. Members, it appears that in some areas the time taken to provide translations is still unacceptably long. The solution ought not to be to ask the committees of the House to delay their work while unduly waiting for a translation to be completed; on the contrary, the Department of the Secretary of State must be made fully aware of the particular needs of legislators so that the required resources are made available in order to meet the translation requirements of the House.

The Hon. Member for Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme) suggested that a mandate be given to the Standing Committee on Management and Members' Services to consider the matter. But may I be permitted, with respect, to indicate to the Hon. Member and the House that the standing committee may already have that power in its general mandate, as provided in Standing Order 96(3)(c), to review:
-and report to the Speaker as well as the Board of Internal Economy, on the administration of the House and the provision of services and facilities to Members-
The fact that the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon and the Hon. Member for Regina West chose to bring their concerns to the attention of their colleagues is a good indication to the Chair that the question of translation services continues to be viewed as fundamental by many Members. Again, I must thank both Hon. Members as well as the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) and the Hon. Member for Saint-Denis for sharing their views with the Chair.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Hnatyshyn that Bill C-54, an Act to amend the Criminal Code and other Acts in consequence thereof, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

Madam Speaker, I rise today to address Bill C-54, an Act to amend the Criminal Code and other Acts in consequence thereof.
I want to begin with perhaps a look at the injustice and the imbalance of the scales of justice inherent and implicit with the application of the Bill. What we have here is an
unbalanced view by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) being presented, to try to counteract the very serious concerns that we have with child pornography, obscenity and violence toward men, women and children. We have as well concerns about human sexuality and its normalcy in society. We have all those groups who have looked at the Bill and see that it is contrary to the basic principles of law that say a defendant is innocent until proven guilty. We can find it no longer acceptable to have this kind of repressive and regressive legislation within our laws.
With respect to that aspect, often there have been individuals who have said that this Bill is right, that it is on target and that it is a response to what the community is asking for. But this Bill has raised a tremendous furor in the artistic and the legal world. There are serious concerns about its propriety. The legislation has not been overlooked in international circles either. I have been told that the fiftieth Congress of the International Writers' Organization, PEN, meeting in Lugan, Sweden, passed a resolution on May 15 expressing concern about this proposed law, especially the section dealing with artistic merit which shifts the burden of proof from the state to the defendant.
One talks about obscenity, pornography and kiddy porn or child porn in this Bill but at the same time we are addressing the issues of erotica. There is an intrusion by the state into the life of people within their own homes. 1 suggest that adult Canadians expect their legislators, their Government and their police to treat them as adults. I suggest also, Madam Speaker, that the conduct of consenting adults in the privacy of their homes is a personal affair and is not the affair of the state. While saying that, Liberals are concerned with recent trends that demonstrate an increase in violence, battering and the number of pornographic books, magazines and literature which depict an untrue picture of sexuality to our young people. Child pornography, violent pornography, and human degradation need tougher legislative sanctions of the type proposed in Bill C-54. I suggest that concern has been raised about the long-term effect of this violent and degrading pornographic material. There are studies to this effect which were conducted on prisoners.
The public needs to be educated against violence to men, women and children, but success depends on how you go about it and how the attitude of Government is reflected in the law. I suggest that pornography needs a much more clear definition. The Government should be prepared to re-examine its definition of erotica and pornography. The Bill tries to cover a garden variety of sex, and that is totally repressive and regressive.
As far as I am concerned, what is really at issue is child pornography and violent pornography, and the definition of erotica. Because of the broad definition in this Bill, erotica is reduced to covering mere nudity; when it is associated with
November 30, 1987

sex, it becomes illegal. I find that unacceptable in today's society. If you read the definition of erotica, it is really enough to blow your mind. It says:
"erotica" means any visual matter a dominant characteristic of which is the depiction, in a sexual context or for the purpose of the sexual stimulation of the viewer, of a human sexual organ, a female breast or the human anal region;
That is a pretty broad definition of the normal facts of life. Under pornography we have a long list of no-nos, many of which I agree with. Yet when you get down to Clause l(a)(vi), it includes:
masturbation or ejaculation not referred to in sub-paragraph (iv), or vaginal, anal or oral intercourse,
I suggest it all depends how those normal daily functions, in many cases, are defined. This is a rather broad sweep to cover what I think the legislation wants to cover, which is undue exploitation. That has been covered in previous legislation but not defined as accurately as one would like. I suggest that this is not the place for that particular definition. I hope that when this Bill goes to committee, this particular clause will be examined much more closely and put in the right place. There should, in any case, also be some improvement in the definition.
I suggest that the obscenity legislation in Canada has been ambiguous, and this is what we are trying to clear up. That is the whole point at issue. Two provisions in our Criminal Code have been employed to prosecute alleged offenders in the past. There was the antiquated "disgusting object" provision, and the obscenity code modified in 1962 as a result of a Supreme Court ruling which called for the inclusion of a community standards test. Then the obscenity provision was amended by Bill C-58 in 1959 to qualify "obscene" as any publication the dominant characteristic of which is undue exploitation of sex. Again that term left considerable room for defence against prosecution, as did the indefinable nature of community standards. These provisions, coupled with Customs and Excise restrictions on obscene materials, and provincial legislation, have helped create a climate of subtle repression of artistic freedom. Yet the lack of definition accorded the terminology used has provoked the Government to outline in sweeping terms what it has deemed pornographic.
The Government seems to have a very difficult time in making definitions. We have seen it in the copyright legislation and we see it again in this Bill. The definition of pornography and erotica is too narrow and vague. That results in the criminalization of sexual activity among consenting adults. I hope all Members of this House plan to have a criminal activity of this sort at some point or another in the near future.
The dominant characteristic in an artist's mind is symbolism. It is character study. It is theme, or other artistic development or expression. Sexual stimulation or the naked body are essential conduits for this artistic intent. Whose perspective decides whether sex is the end or merely the means to an end?
Criminal Code
If you read Clauses 159.4, 159.5 and 159.6 you have to ask yourself, what did the Department of Justice have in mind? They are regressive, repressive and unbelievable. I call them the fig-leaf clauses. They are talking about exhibition of erotica to persons under the age of 18 years of age, yet they define erotica as normal sexual behaviour. I am not talking about violence and other than tender loving care, as we think about it in today's world. That is not what the intent was, but that is the way they wrote the Bill. It talks about the exhibition, or sale or rental of erotica to persons under 18 years of age. Then it talks about what the offences are going to be and how they are to be defined. You have to prove that the accused took all responsible steps to ensure there was no erotica in the thing sold, rented or offered for sale, and that it has artistic merit.
Having to define and defend artistic merit, and being guilty until proven innocent, is a rather strange concept in British common law and certainly not what we are used to. I suggest that when you have to prove your innocence, it becomes a strain, a drain on time and dollars. Lord only knows that our artists are not exactly the best paid in our society. Yet it is not enough to prove that the purpose is artistic merit. If the art falls below what is called the artistic merit threshold-and who determines that-there is no defence. It is not up to the Crown to prove there was no artistic merit. The accused must establish that there is artistic merit once the Crown has proved that the work falls within the broad definition of erotica. This definition is too narrow, excludes the act of love between two consenting adults, and all the normal parts of the body, which are in themselves, as well as the act of making love, legal. There is something rather strange in the whole approach.
The erotica clause has an interpretation which now classifies intercourse as pornography. The definition of pornography is thus made to stand on depictions that may simply be offensive to some members of society. I hope, first, that it is not offensive to most of us and, second, that the legislators will clean up their act in terms of that wording. I do not think that was their intent.
The reverse onus provisions of Bill C-54, which require artists to prove artistic merit, place an unjustifiable hardship upon the artistic community. Where they have to prove that the consumer is under the age of 18 there is no artistic defence. The following example used by Pierre Berton demonstrates the silliness behind some of these definitions.
If the Charlottetown Festival revived Johnny Belinda, it would have to plead artistic merit in order to enact the rape scene. The same would apply to Les liaison dangereuses. It would not matter whether the actor or actress in these instances were fully clothed or whether the rape was clearly simulated. Moreover, if there is a single 17-year-old in the audience at a family festival, artistic merit goes out the window as a defence and it is pornography.

November 30, 1987
Criminal Code
Therefore, if you show any sexual activity on the screen or on the stage which involves anyone who even looks as though he or she is under 18 years of age, there is no defence. You cannot say that it is educational or artistic even if the part of a teenager is played by a 25-year-old. You are still guilty of depicting pornography. Do you think that is the purpose of this legislation or is it only that they did not understand what they were writing?
The Actors' Equity Association believes that such provisions intended to prevent child pornography would effectively prohibit productions of coming of age material and material dealing with the topic of sexual abuse and exploitation of children. For example, the internationally acclaimed play by Dennis Foon, Feeling Yes, Feeling No, concerning sexual abuse prevention would be in jeopardy.
Not only are live theatre and movies affected, but so are art galleries and museums. For example, the painting now presently hanging in the National Gallery of Canada by Paul Peel entitled After the Bath might well be in contravention of Bill C-54 as it shows naked children clearly under the age of 18. It would be hard to imagine the Crown charging the National Gallery, but this might well arise if the Bill remains unaltered.
We may be able to prevent that by putting up a sign indicating that the painting is erotica or if we wrap it in an opaque material. Of course, we would then have to peek behind the opaque material to find out what the erotica was. There are things in this Bill which I find absolutely mind blowing.
I believe that the defence of artistic merit is unworkable in its present form. It represents a significant departure from the normal approach to criminal sanctions contained in other parts of the Criminal Code. It is a sort of looking glass approach which creates a philosophic and legal bias in favour of the Crown against the rights of the defendant. Long ago Canadians elected to follow the British tradition which prefers to allow a few guilty people to remain free rather than deprive an innocent person of liberty.
Clarke Rogers, artistic director of Toronto's Theatre Passe Muraille, sums up well the feelings of many creators on this point with the following statement:
The inability to distinguish between works of art and gross pornography is a social failure, not an artist's problem. Yet we become the scapegoats. All that you do is intimidate artists and encourage self-censorship in the name of economic survival. If you're constantly being threatened by big legal bills, creativity is bound to suffer.
I am sure that all Members of this House would agree with that. Theatre and art gallery owners will be wary of presenting any work which may appear to violate pornography laws as interpreted by the local law enforcement authorities.
I would like the House to give serious thought to some of the concerns which are being expressed by other groups. The Canadian Artist's Representation association believes that
they have been placed upon the fringes of society, unable to enjoy freedom of expression through Bill C-54. They said:
-it is a part of our function as artists to question society; to hold a mirror up to society; to analyze our own shortcomings; and to explore the more remote territories of human experience. We rejoice in our senses. We do not create "pretty pictures" or amuse. Because we are not society's clowns and because we are vitally important to our society's well-being any restriction placed upon freedom of artistic expression will be a serious jeopardy to us and our society as a whole.
We believe that such restrictions upon our rights and freedom of artistic expression are not demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society. Have we as a society elevated moral and political censorship to the status of a social idea?
I think not, Madam Speaker, and I know that my Party does not think so and we are looking toward proper amendment.
I would like to bring to your attention an exchange which I had in committee with Mr. Maceroia, the Director General of the National Film Board. I asked him whether he thought that we could make and show Le declin de I'empire americain under the new pornography Bill. As you know, that film won all kinds of awards.

Do you think that the new legislation on pornography would allow you today to produce and show the movie The Decline of the American Empirel No, replied Mr. Maceroia. Did you point it out to the Minister? Yes, said Mr. Maceroia. Did you discuss the matter with the Minister of Justice? Yes and not only with respect to The Decline of the American Empire. We are now drawing up a list of motion pictures taken out of our catalogue to be in a positiom to advise the Minister that it would be impossible to produce such movies with the new bill.
We went on dealing with various findings which show that the contents of some of the provisions of the bill should be amended.

Mr. Pelletier, the Acting Secretary General of the National Museums, said that they saw an earlier version of the Bill and that it had been changed somewhat recently. A document was prepared within the corporation by their policy people examining the implications and they were worried. They brought that to the attention of the Minister.
The Canadian Independent Record Production Association said that it is are concerned that the present Bill may be akin to using a sledgehammer to crack a nut and may well result in creating more anomalies and abuses than it cures.
Objections come from Brick Books, the League of Canadian Poets, the Toronto Arts Council, the Playwrights Union, Harry Cuff Publications, the Canadian Library Association, the Association of Canadian Booksellers, the Photographers Gallery, and the Royal Canadian College of Organists. I could go on and on. I plead through you, Madam Speaker, with the Government to amend the Bill and section off the part on erotica which is totally unacceptable, regressive, and repressive in today's modern society.
November 30, 1987

Madam Speaker, the Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone) and I, I am sure, agree on how difficult the problem of pornography is. She and I were members of the Special Committee on Child Care. I remember having a very serious discussion with her on some of the difficulties in prosecuting pornography cases. We discussed the case of Penthouse magazine which, depending on your point of view, is soft core pornography. However, in at least one instance it was convicted. It was very difficult to get a conviction because, as I am sure the Hon. Member would agree, the present provisions in the Criminal Code are inadequate. They are vague, in some cases to the point of being almost unenforcible. Therefore, all of us share the problem of what to do with this very difficult problem. The Government has made an attempt to do so in Bill C-54, with which I am pleased and proud to be associated. It defines for the first time in the Criminal Code exactly what pornography is.
If the Hon. Member and her Party and Members of the New Democratic Party do not like the definition, I suggest that it is incumbent upon them to give us their definition of pornography. It has been my experience on the justice committee for a couple of years that while everyone agrees there is a problem with street soliciting, pornography and sexual exploitation, whenever the Government attempts to come to grips with the problem and put a definition before Parliament, the Opposition states they do not like it because it is either too narrow, too broad, too vague or too regressive.
I suggest to them, as 1 have suggested to witnesses who have appeared the committee, that if they have a better definition, let us see it in the committee. I sit on the legislative committee with the Member for Mount Royal. Let us see their definition and have an opportunity to compare. We are all trying to control the same problem.
I have heard comments in this debate that the definition is too repressive, too vague or too narrow. Let us see what the NDP and Liberals have to propose. I think that is only fair. If they have as many reservations as they say they do about what I believe to be an excellent piece of legislation, let us see what they have to offer.

Madam Speaker, I think that is a constructive observation. 1 recommend that the Hon. Member reread the Fraser and Badgley reports which contain some definitions that I believe all three Parties could address.
I believe that the present provisions are inadequate. One can see on the cover of Hustler magazine a woman's legs sticking out of a mincemeat grinder, with other parts of the body coming through, or the picture of a woman bound and hanging on a Christmas tree. I do not believe that is very appetizing or what Canadians want.
I agree with the Hon. Member and I stated in my speech that we need change. I also recommended that we need to consider other changes. I sincerely hope we can agree upon a
Criminal Code
description that will remove the particular reference to masturbation, ejaculation, vaginal, anal and oral intercourse. I think those are totally unacceptable and out of place.

Madam Speaker, I am concerned about the comment of the Hon. Member for Niagara Falls (Mr. Nicholson). He is trying to pretend that there have not been constructive and specific alternatives put forward, which have attracted broad support from women's groups, the artistic community, others who are concerned about censorship, human rights, and people concerned about pornography, particularly against children.
The Hon. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone) just mentioned the Fraser committee report. This report came to grips with the issues and the Hon. Member is being deceptive and misleading in suggesting that constructive proposals have not been put forward not only by Members of my Party and the Liberal Party, but from what appears to be a much broader basis of support than the proposals being put up by the Government which seem generally to be put before the Conservative Party by REAL Women and a few other groups that are excessively right wing and do not represent the mainstream of Canadian society.
My question to the Hon. Member is related to her comments on the film The Decline of the American Empire. That is an award-winning, commercially successful film and it represents part of the coming-of-age of the Canadian cinema. I agree with her view that this film would not in fact be able to be shown in any way in Canada according to Bill C-54.
The lovely film entitled Lies my Father Told Me dealt sensitively and evocatively with Montreal some 60 years ago. It is based on Mordecai Richler's book. I presume that scenes which involved children learning a bit about life by finding out that the woman down the street made her living as a prostitute because of the Depression would not be allowable according to the Bill. As I understand it, even a chance depiction of a female breast in a television production which came to us from France, the United Kingdom or other countries that do not have the puritan standards which the Conservatives want to impose upon us would in fact be treated as erotica and could not be shown to children, meaning people up to the age of 18. Therefore, a whole range of television productions, including drama, science, and art from other countries would effectively be banned from Canadian television.
Is that how we are proceeding into the 1990s with the Conservatives? Are those the kinds of standards that a repressive minority is trying to impose on a majority who are concerned about pornography but do not at the same time want their ability to function as adults to be seriously impaired by such a ridiculous restriction?

Madam Speaker, my hon. colleague is right on target. Not only will it affect the choice at the film theatre and the selections on our TV screen, it will also affect those of us who go to the public libraries for books. It will certainly
