Adjournment Debate
have an effect on the paintings in our museums. I hope the Minister of Justice will not be insensitive to this restrictive and repressive Conservative view and will make the necessary changes.

Madam Speaker, I respect and fully understand the importance of the arguments that the Hon. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone) has been making. As a former journalist, may I associate myself with her argument that the definition of undue exploitation of sex is far too ambiguous. One could drive a legal transport truck through its passages, as most people have since this particular definition came out.
Since school children, including my 16-year old son, are returning home at this hour, I respectfully request that we defer all of the explicit references such as those which have been made by the Hon. Member for Mount Royal and the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy), until we get to committee. I believe that is where we can iron out some of the real problems, including the definition of undue exploitation of sex.
Would the Hon. Member not agree that the House is in agreement that this matter should be referred to the committee at once and dealt with there in the more informal surroundings that are not within ear-shot? I would respectfully suggest that Hon. Members please refer this matter to committee at once and let the committee deal with the more lurid details.

Madam Speaker, in acknowledging my hon. colleague's concerns for the nebulous aspects of the present Bill, and also respecting his sense of personal discomfort with some of the wording referred to in the Bill, I would, however, bring to his attention that as a mother and a grandmother- and, by the way a grandmother of my third grandchild-1 have always referred to the parts of the body by the way they are defined. I have not used itsy bitsy cutesy phrases. I do not know what is wrong with using natural and normal phrases. Human sexuality is a beautiful part of life. Without it we all would not be here, nor would we have a future. I would suggest it is not an aberration and it is not difficult to discuss with one's children. I would hope that the kind of books which would be accessible in the libraries and schools of this land, and the kind of films we will use, will be such that our children can protect themselves and be able to make an intelligent decision as to how to handle themselves. I hope that will be carefully and clearly thought through in the legislative committee.

subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED
speechtext: It is my duty, pursuant to Standing Order 66, to inform the House that the questions to be raised tonight at the time of adjournment are as follows: the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Redway)- Immigration-Senate Committee's Report on Terrorism; the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald)- Health-Acid rain-Health hazard query/Request for stricter pollution emission standards; the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson)-External Affairs-Victims of brainwashing experiments funded by CIA/Request for financial assistance in seeking legal redress.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Hnatyshyn that Bill C-54, an Act to amend the Criminal Code and other Acts in consequence thereof, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee; and on the amendment of Mr. Robinson (p. 11291).

Madam Speaker, I am participating in this debate because I am concerned that Bill C-54 is just a clone of Bill C-l 14, which was presented by the Government a year or more ago and which was found so seriously wanting, it had to be quickly withdrawn. It had to be quickly withdrawn because there was a general feeling in the community of Canada as a whole that the views of the narrow so-called moral majority were in fact not acceptable views to be imposed upon Canadians as a whole when it came to the question of pornography.
My Party, as our justice critic has already indicated, has in convention considered the matter seriously. We have devoted a lot of time to this particular question and we have indicated that we do believe there needs to be changes in Canadian law. Quite specifically, we have said that the law should be changed to define as pornography, material which condones violence, coercion, abuse and degradation in its depiction of human beings and this should include the production and distribution of such material whether in film, video, print or any other form. We also said that the definition of pornography should include material which portrays or promotes the sexual exploitation of children. We called for severe penalties for offenders. In response to the Hon. Member for Niagara Falls (Mr. Nicholson), therefore, the New Democrats have at the very least been very specific.
November 30, 1987

What we are debating right now is a reasoned amendment on second reading of this particular Bill which was proposed by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson). The amendment states we should decline to give second reading to Bill C-54 because it fails to clearly define pornography in the way I have just mentioned. It does not distinguish pornography from material of an artistic, literary, educational or scientific nature in a fashion acceptable to the Canadian public, including artists. I suppose part of the reason I am participating in this debate is to say, let us be sensible and relax a bit while at the same time recognizing that new laws on pornography, particularly on child pornography, are needed.
There is something that is deeply troubling to me. If I turn on the television some evening when I am rather tired, in the course of that evening I can see 8, 10 or 15 acts of extreme violence, the kind of acts which lead people to think that we live in a violent society and older people to think that they are hardly safe to walk on the streets at night, something which, at least in Canada, is certainly far from the truth. Yet those kinds of depictions of violence, which are quite out of sorts with what actually happens in our daily lives in a country which is relatively peaceful in relation to violence and which has a low murder rate, and so on, go unpunished. At the same time, the least passing look at a female breast on television will, according to this law, be considered erotica and because it is shown to children, there will be no artistic defence, as I understand, and in fact might lead to up to two years of imprisonment. In certain cases, some of the definitions of pornography can lead to up to 10 years in imprisonment.
The way in which artists help to perhaps define societies and what societies might become is interesting to me. I would draw to the attention of Hon. Members and to the attention of the viewers who are watching this debate, including some of the 16-year-olds referred to by the Hon. Member for Hamilton- Wentworth (Mr. Scott), Margaret Atwood's recent novel, the Hand Maid's Tale, which I read a few months ago. It depicts a society in the 1990s with severe sexual repression, and what happens when a society has severe sexual repressions along those lines. People who are rich, powerful and well connected then go and do on the side what they are telling the population as a whole it cannot do.
It is equally ironic that we should be discussing this Bill not that long after the collapse in utter disarray of the moral majority in the United States. We find out that this is not just something that happens in fiction but in real life. People like Jimmy and Tammy Bakker were playing around in all kinds of ways, rather similar to the kinds of things that occur in soap operas on daytime television, which those two condemned so roundly. To put it mildly, they failed to live up to the standards of sexual conformity which they were seeking to inculcate in their followers.
The entire right wing in the United states showed a total incapacity to live up to basic standards of ethics and laws and indulged, condoned or were involved in such things as Irangate
Criminal Code
and the various kinds of shenanigans which went on there. They showed themselves totally unprepared to live up to the most basic of constitutional law as it is understood in the United States. To bring us back to the debate here, as you are about to do, Madam Speaker, these are the same people who have been passing messages to the moral majority, to the new right wing in Canada, saying we need the kind of legislation which is represented in Bill C-54. If we have that kind of hypocrisy taking place, we are going to get lousy results. At the same time, excessively repressive legislation, I believe, is going to backfire in all kinds of unpleasant and undesirable ways.
My colleague, and former colleague in the Press Gallery, the Hon. Member for Hamilton-Wentworth, suggested he was concerned about what his 16-year-old son might see on the way home from school. Some years ago I took two or three of my teenage sons, at that point in their mid-teens, to see the movie Fame in Toronto. That movie, for people who have not seen it, is a movie about young men and women at the high school for the performing arts in Brooklyn. It is not about just growing up artistically but growing up as human beings. Some make it and some fail. One of the scenes which I can depict without trouble on daytime television is of a young girl who wants to be in films and is tricked into going for what is said to be a film test. In fact, some cruel adult makes her strip in front of a camera for a so-called film test when in fact it is just erotic exploitation of a young person. I ask myself if it would be better for a teenage girl living and growing up in Toronto who wants to get into films to learn the lesson to watch out for that kind of thing by seeing a film or to have it happen to her in person. The answer is obvious.
During the course of that film there was the scene where the boys in the school happen to find a way of looking into the girls' washroom. In what I thought was a rather innocent and amusing way they saw one or two of the girls changing. Again, that is something which happens in the life of every teenager, I would assume. It happened in my life and I am sure it happened even in the boyhood or teenage years of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn). That, too, would attract the attention of the moral protectors under Bill C-54.
In fact, we could not get into the film Fame. We could not take our teenage kids into that movie despite the fact it had a very solid, positive message about growing up in all kinds of ways, and in ways which are real to teenage men and women. Later, as a consequence, we sneaked our children into the film. We broke Ontario's film censorship laws and took our children into an unrestricted movie that was part of a double-header, and when the first film ended they stayed and watched the second film and received the types of benefits-
Breaking the law?

The Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Oberle) states "breaking the law". If there

November 30, 1987
Criminal Code
are bad laws, sooner or later people will start to find ways of changing them.
I wish to cite another example. The Tin Drum, an artistic film of the highest merit, one of the finest films that I have seen from continental Europe in the past 15 or 20 years, was banned by the Ontario film censor. As Leader of the Ontario New Democrats, I took a group, we defied the law, and attended a special screening of that particular film. As someone who had spent some time in post-war Germany, I was astonished at how effectively that film, using all types of literary and artistic devices, transmitted the terrible and awful things that had happened in Germany before, during, and after the war. Because the central character in that film is an adult with only the growth of a child, it would not be permitted under Bill C-54.
I would venture to say that a reasonable number of Conservative MPs from the Toronto area have seen the production of O Calcutta. I believe it has been running in Toronto for seven or eight years. I think that it is a silly production, but I am not sure whether the moral fibre of Toronto has gone permanently to the dogs because of a stage production which features nudity and which is essentially preoccupied with sex.
In all of this, I look at the Bill and ask myself, what is really different from Bill C-114? The Library of Parliament has kindly prepared a summary which I have looked at. I wish to read the definitions of simple pornography.
In Bill C-l 14 was outlawed pornography which was defined as visual matter showing vaginal, anal, or oral intercourse; ejaculation, sexually violent behaviour, bestiality, incest, necrophilia, masturbation, or other sexual activity. That was particularly criticized because of the reference to "other sexual activity" which could presumably mean giving your cousin a kiss.
However, Bill C-54 is almost the same. It refers to bestiality, incest, or necrophilia; it refers to masturbation or ejaculation, and then it refers to vaginal, anal, or oral intercourse.
The Hon. Member for Hamilton-Wentworth stated that the details will be fixed up in committee. Let us address the principle involved. The fact is that the Bill is a clone of the previous Bill. The Bill means that a great deal of normal-let us put it quite bluntly-human activity, which I venture to say every Member of Parliament has taken part in, and hopefully with a great deal of pleasure, anticipation, and fond remembrance is dirty. That is true of the adult population. Members of Parliament, our constituents, and all of us would not have been here if it had not been for human sexual activity. We must be careful before we turn around and say to our children and everybody else that somehow everything in this area is dirty. It is not.
Activities which involve violence and sex are dirty. Activities that involve brutality and degradation of one human being by another are dirty and should be stopped. Activities which involve the exploitation of children in a sexual sense are dirty
and should be outlawed. But for goodness sake let us have some sense of proportion in all of this.
I find it astonishing that a Government could have brought in a Bill which responded to widespread concerns about pornography, and then narrowed the definition and made it so restrictive, repressive, and objectionable that virtually every important group representing women, as well as the artistic community and people concerned about censorship, has spoken against Bill C-54.
ACTRA, the AIDS Committee of Toronto, the Canada Council, the Canadian Committee Against Customs Censorship, the Canadian Conference of the Arts, the Coalition for the Right to View, Feminists Against Censorship, the International Women's Day Committee in Toronto, Media People for Social Responsibility, the National Action Committee on the Status of Women, the Ontario Association of Art Galleries, the Ontario Coalition for Abortion Clinics, the Ontario Film and Video Appreciation Society, the International Writers' Organization, PEN, the Periodical Marketers of Canada, the Toronto Arts Council, and the Writers' Union of Canada. That is one range of groups. What about the media? The Globe and Mail, La Presse, Le Devoir, The Ottawa Citizen, the Toronto Star, The Toronto Sun, and The Vancouver Sun have all spoken out against the legislation in Bill C-54.
What is being done in this Bill will mean, among other things, I suppose that the police can come along and either if by hazard or with a search warrant can go into my library and look and see if I have any documents which I made about 25 years ago which are deemed to be child pornography.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext: That is an exaggeration.

I am not exaggerating, Madam Speaker. The Hon. Member suggests that I am exaggerating. A book which involves children in one part of the book and which talks about intercourse in another part of the book could be deemed to be child pornography, and I could probably be jailed for having that book in my library, even though I inherited it from my father who bought it 30 or 40 years ago. That is the situation.
Nonsense.

If it is nonsense, then we should change the Bill so it is not a possibility. I speak with passion. A former Prime Minister said that the state had no place in the bedrooms of the nation. I wonder if the state has a place in the libraries or the book rooms of the nation, along the lines of what are presently suggested.
Would a book which talks to children about sex in a positive and sensitive way, for example, Show Me, be permissible or not? Will we be in a situation where every work of art and every work that touches upon sexual subjects and which has been published in Canada over the last 50 years will risk being taken before the courts? Many of those books are still in circulation, if they are not in first printing, perhaps they are in used bookstores. Used booksellers and booksellers in general
November 30, 1987

and people like myself who have a substantial library will have to look through all of our books to see whether or not they are all right.
What about Arabian Nights? Could I be taken to court because I have a copy of Thousand and One Nights in my library, and which certainly involves sex? It involves young people under 18 or apparently under the age of 18.
Read the Bill.

The Hon. Member says to read the Bill. I will read the Bill. They will know that the test of artistic merit is not a test which has to be proven by the Crown, it is the defence which has to be proven by the accused. I could be dragged through the courts and forced to pay thousands of dollars in legal fees in order to prove that Arabian Nights had artistic merit, and therefore-
Absolutely not.

The Hon. Member states "absolutely not". Well, let him change the Bill.
In addition, if somewhere in Thousand and One Nights there was a concubine in a harem, who, according to the book might have been less than 18 years old, then there would be no defence of artistic merit. That is what is in the Bill.
Now I simply say to the Hon. Members opposite in the Conservative Party, is this the ridiculous type of thing that they are trying to suggest? They will make this country into a laughing stock around the world when people look at what is being put forward in Bill C-54. I do not think that I can accept that.
I repeat that I believe, as my Party believes, that it is necessary to have a redefinition of pornography. What we have now has proven to be inadequate and unacceptable. I have no problem saying that. However, it is crazy to put a legitimate artist in a situation where, for example, he or she may have to go to court and with limited resources defend whether or not a work of art has artistic merit. We are all put in a situation where the entire Bill will inevitably be challenged under the Charter of Rights and Freedoms because of its restraints on freedom of expression. 1 believe it incontrovertibly goes far beyond what is necessary in a free and democratic society concerned about pornography as the degradation of women, about pornography where violence and sex are linked, or about pornography where perhaps males are being encouraged to indulge in acts which are demeaning to the human dignity of another person.
This is why I endorse and support the reasoned amendment moved by my colleague. I hope Hon. Members will join with me in saying to the Government, as many in the media have said, "You blew it again". The Fraser and the Badgley committees have come up with some positive alternatives. Let us go back to those and come up with a Bill which will have
Criminal Code
broad consensus support, particularly from mainstream organizations representing women across Canada.

Madam Speaker, I have looked at the definition of pornography, and I have heard the allegations of the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy) that Members of the House were engaged in activities which would be wrong under the Bill. The Hon. Member felt that it was common for Members of the House to be involved in degrading acts in a sexual context, including a person who treats any other person as an animal or object, who engages in acts of bondage, who penetrates with an object the vagina or anus of the person, who defecates, urinates, or ejaculates on to other persons, or who is involved in bestiality, incest, or necrophilia which, for the information of the House, is intercourse with a dead body.
I thought that we had honourable people in the House, but it may be that we are going too far in this Bill, because the standard of conduct of the Member opposite and his colleagues in the NDP would treat these matters as ordinary matters. Would the Hon. Member like to tell us which Members of the House are involved in defecating and ejaculating over other people, in bestiality, incest, or necrophilia?

Madam Speaker, I think the Hon. Member knows that in the first place the acts to which he has just referred have always been illegal. I would hope that no Members have indulged in such acts.
However Clause 6 of the Bill indicates that any visual matter which shows vaginal intercourse is pornography. In addition, if it is done or is associated in any way with a person under the age of 18 years, not only is it then child pornography but also the defence of artistic merit is not admissible in the courts. For example, an actor involved in a stage presentation which was deemed to have met those particular criteria could be subject to a jail sentence for simply having participated.
I must assume that that is what the Government intended when it included that in the Bill. As a consequence, between that and the very restrictive rules relative to erotica, the Government has included an important area of human expression in which presumably all Members or almost all have engaged with pleasure and certainly without which none of the Members of the House would be here, except for perhaps a few members of the Conservative Party who may have been the products of virgin birth. To suggest that that is not part of normal human expression and to treat it as dirty is wrong.
Madam Speaker, I wonder whether the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy) could expand a little on a point which he made earlier in his speech regarding-

Oh, oh!

November 30, 1987
Criminal Code

Madam Speaker, Hon. Members on the government side seem to have a lot to say. I hope they will rise to speak on the issue.
Prior to being elected I was involved in the field of corrections, probation, and parole. I happen to know something of what I speak in terms of those persons who unfortunately have serious sexual deviations and problems resulting in all cases from childhood and childhood training. They are not instinctual behavioural problems associated with human sexuality.
I wonder whether the Hon. Member would expand for a moment or two on the value, not only to young people but to humanity generally, of learning from film and literature about human sexuality.
It is only through these kinds of learning experiences that standards of acceptable sexual behaviour can be learned. Sexuality in terms of what is acceptable sociologically in Canadian society and elsewhere in the world is only learned through film, literature, and so on. I should like to hear further remarks from the Hon. Member, because I think Canadians generally are interested in what kind of law is most appropriate to provide the kind of peaceful and sane society in which we would all like to live and raise our children.

Madam Speaker, I thank my colleague for a good and sensitive question.
I have three sons. The youngest is now 19 years of age. I have watched them and their friends learn about life. They have always seemed to choose the hard way, but that is their affair. I have watched them grow up and gradually begin to make friends with young women. Some of them have now reached the point of adulthood where they are sharing their lives with young women.
One does not suddenly become a sexual being the moment one turns 18, which I believe is the essential picture suggested in the Bill. Communications between parents and teenagers, as I well know, are not always easy. Often it is difficult, no matter how much we would like it to happen, for parents to be the only source of information and guidance for our young people.
This is why we have story-tellers, and we have had storytellers in society since the days when a few savages sat around a camp-fire half frozen in the northern nights of Canada. Today our story-tellers are novelists. They produce pictures, films, and plays. They are the story-tellers of our times.
As we said in our Party resolution, material which promotes the sexual exploitation of children and is violent or degrading in a sexual context toward children is clearly inadmissible. However, what about sensitive material dealing with children reaching out as they begin to recognize that they are sexual beings or dealing with the difficulties faced by young girls who menstruate these days at the age of 12 or 13? It may be as many as 10 years or 12 years in society today before they decide to get married. They must contend with a whole range
of feelings, responsibilities, potentials, and risks, as we increasingly have a more egalitarian society which more equally understands the obligations of men and women in terms of preventing conception and in terms of raising children. These kinds of things must be felt by boys as well once they reach the ages of 12 years or 13 years. Through older brothers and sisters they cannot help but be aware of burgeoning sexuality. These are the facts. We cannot take away those facts by pretending they do not exist.
I have a friend who teaches in a school with a very repressive, may I say, religious point of view under which only religion teachers are entitled to talk to 14, 15, and 16 year old kids about sex. This does not stop the fact that they are brim-full of hormones and that they are trying to learn about these things. It is a very difficult matter which needs to be approached sensitively. It does not require the sledge-hammer approach which I am afraid we find in Bill C-54.
It is a difficult area. Although I welcome changes in the law, I do not welcome these changes because I do not think they adequately come to grips with what is needed in terms of helping young men and women on their way to adulthood in sexuality as well as in other things.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Lise Bourgault (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to rise today to deal with this major Bill aimed at correcting a situation which has existed for the past 20 years and which has been deteriorating year after year.
Madam Speaker, I must admit it is not easy for a person raised in a very conservative family and under a rather puritan system to deal with such issues as sexuality, pornography and bestiality. When I was attending school, we simply did not talk about those things, and although my father and mother were very good parents, they always had a lot of difficulty talking openly about sex.
Ever since we came into office three years ago, Madam Speaker, it is clear that each time legislation was introduced, NDP and Liberal members have always whined about the new calamity which was being visited on the Canadian public. They always exaggerated, describing any new piece of legislation as terrible and frightening. Whether it is the famous Bill C-22 or other Bills which they claimed would result in hundreds of thousands of jobs being lost, while on the contrary they created a great many. In short, Hon. Members opposite always find Government legislation terrible, but in the end people adapt to it. A Government certainly cannot hope to please the Canadian people 100 per cent. I do not believe that those who make money selling pornography exploiting children and, of course, women-as women, we have always been victimized by this somewhat uncommon moneymaking exercise-will be pleased with this Bill. That is understandable.
November 30, 1987

Madam Speaker, I remember that, not so long ago, when the Government introduced Bill C-49, we heard exactly the same arguments from hon. Members opposite. I realize today that municipalities finally got over it and people involved in prostitution have changed their attitude. I suggest that people will do like- wise with Bill C-54.
First of all, the House should remember that in 1978, the Liberal Government of the day introduced a similar Bill-1 do not know what it did with it-but nothing came of it. It is easy to be a Liberal today and speak against Bill C-54-after having been in office for 25 years and unable to come up with legislation to curb prostitution and the pornographic plague from which, as I see it, stem other types of violence on which I will be commenting later on.
In 1981 or 1982 ex-Minister of Justice McGuigan had also made an attempt to introduce a minor amendment to the Criminal Code, but he finally came to the conclusion that dealing with this kind of issue was not a popular endeavour within his own Party, so he opted for commissioning the Fraser committee. Madam Speaker, we have to be honest enough to admit today that after so many years-I think this need to be said-there was a lack of leadership in governments, and the situation has degenerated to such an extent that Canadians can no longer tolerate what has happened and is still happening today in society.
Madam Speaker, I am glad to see that a Conservative Government which has more faith in traditional and family values has had the courage to introduce this Bill which is the logical complement of Bill C-15. At long last we have found ways to make sure that in future our Canadian society will show respect for the dignity of women and the integrity of our children.
Madam Speaker, the Bill sends a crystal-clear message to men and women who exploit children: such behaviour will no longer be tolerated. Our children have the right to be protected against such exploitation and such prejudices. All of us here in the House must see to it that children are sheltered from degradation and sexual violence.
Madam Speaker, very often, the movies, pornographic material and other disgusting things being showned to men and women who view this kind of material will cause a simple fantasy in the mind of these people to degenerate into an act of violence or even murder. One just has to read newspapers that specialize in murder stories, for instance Alio Police or Photo Police, to see that very often there is pornographic material involved in cases of murder or sexual assault on children or women. One can easily imagine how a person who has access to this violent material, especially if that person is young and unarmed, if I can use that phrase, how a teenager can be traumatized and how this type of material can encourage him or her to do the same thing.
Personally, Madam Speaker, I would like all pornographic material including movies and any other kind of pornographic material to be accessible only to adult persons. In other words,
Criminal Code
one should not be able to view or buy any of these things in book stores, not even the so-called adult movies. It is so easy nowadays to rent a videotape. And when one tries to draw the line between pornographic movies and so-called erotica, it is easy to make up definitions that do not mean anything in reality.
What we have here is an amendment to the Bill that doesn't mean anything, because the amendment proposed by the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson), who is the official critic of the New Democratic Party on the matter of justice, provides for . . . actually, it does not provide anything. If the amendment is passed, it will mean that nothing more will be done and that the Bill would have to be reintroduced and studied all over again. This would bring about confusion to no end and ultimately there would be no answer to the Fraser and Badgley Committees.
Madam Speaker, the Bill provides for innovative and useful changes. To start with, it gives a clear and detailed definition of pornography that contrasts with the present legislation. That is important and must be underlined. The present legislation defines an obscene publication as follows: any publication a dominant characteristic of which is the undue exploitation of sex or of sex and one or more of the following subjects, namely violence, etc.
Presently, artists and writers must deal with a very vague definition of the word "obscene" and they have but one available defence, that is to serve the public interest. Although the artistic value is taken into account upon determining whether there has been undue exploitation, it is not by itself an excuse. At that level, Bill C-54 is a significant and genuine improvement.
Madam Speaker, a number of observers have suggested that Bill C-54 goes too far on the grounds that writings can encourage or promote sexual conduct involving children or for that matter any degrading or violent sexual behaviour. Some librarians believe that the provision in the Criminal Code dealing with obscenity does not apply to writings, as against Bill C-54.
I submit, Madam Speaker, that those people although they may be well meaning are mistaken. That provision of the Criminal Code clearly and specifically applies to written material. There is no doubt about that, Madam Speaker. Librarians and authors should not only realize that writings have been subjected to the Criminal Code for a number of years, but also appreciate that this Government is dealing with the matter of writings in a more subdued way.
Finally, anyone with artistic or literary concerns should note the improvement in Bill C-54, as against the legislation introduced by the former Minister of Justice in June 1986.
Madam Speaker, it is my view that for partisan reasons they are indulging in hairsplitting. It is my very honest belief that we must trust Canadians. I am sure, Madam Speaker, that you and I know very well the difference between erotica and

November 30, 1987
Criminal Code
pornography. I am also sure that any judge who would have to rule on that is quite capable of drawing the line between a movie that depicts normal sexual activity for educational purposes and a movie that depicts a sexual act for pornographic purposes, in other words that deviates from the normal sexual act in order to make it attractive for viewers, that goes further and uses some kind of violence, performing the sexual act in such a manner that it be not viewed as a normal sexual act. That is clear in Bill C-54.
Suggesting, as they do, contrary to the Bill, that erotica and pornography are ill-defined amounts to running with the hare and hunting with the hounds. In fact, it means opposing the legislation while being in favour, but this is something we have known for a long time, Madam Speaker, since 1984 the Opposition parties do not know where they stand. As for us, we know where we stand; Bill C-54 states our position. The Liberals and the New Democrats do not know where they stand. They agree with the Bill, but they do not agree with it. They move amendments which would have us withdraw the Bill and begin the entire process all over again, and it is long and difficult and would involve negotiations and discussions which would not achieve anything.
In my opinion, Madam Speaker, the arguments of the women's groups are being used inaccurately. Some have said that the women's groups are against the Bill. It is not true. They are not against the Bill. Quite the opposite. The simple fact is that, like other groups, certain women's groups have expressed an opinion about the definition. The committee to which this Bill will be referred will certainly be able to make recommendations about the definition which concerns the opponents of this Bill. However, they are not opposed to the provisions on child pornography or to the provisions dealing with other matters. They do not even oppose the Bill because of the definition. They have simply expressed their concern about the definition of pornography and erotica.
Madam Speaker, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) should be congratulated for having finally introduced Bill C-54. As the Hon. Members will certainly recall, Bill C-15, which also dealt with sexual offences against children, was passed by this House last June. If Hon. Members are honest, they will recognize that the Conservative Government has responded adequately to the recommendations of the Fraser and Badgley commissions. If they want to be honest intellectually and otherwise, they will also admit that the Government and the Minister of Justice deserve our congratulations for having finally adressed this issue.
Madam Speaker, I am looking at my colleague for Niagara Falls (Mr. Nicholson). I shall never forget that, when I was a member of the committee considering Bill C-49 on prostitution, the mayor and pressure groups from Niagara Falls came before the committee to speak about the ills of prostitution. A question was asked of the mayor of Niagara about pornographic material. In his mind and in the opinion of the groups that appeared before the committee examining Bill C-49 on prostitution, pornography was the starting point for all kinds
of violence. Any way one looked at it, some pornographic material, a film, a magazine, articles, could always be traced back as the source of violence.
Madam Speaker, I do not think there is any Member who does not recall the horrors inflicted on some children by maniacs, as they are called, because they are very sick people. At the hearings or trials, it was once again clearly demonstrated that those people got the idea of committing such acts of violence from something they read or from viewing pornographic movies.
Something had to be done since we are in 1987. That issue has gone on for the last 20 years. It was about time a government stood up and came up with a bill that is not one hundred percent perfect, of course, but that takes into consideration the public concerns at large. And I am sure, Madam Speaker, that Canadian men and women will give credit to the Governement for having dared speak up, in this piece of legislation, and bring forward a bill that will deal with and, hopefully, put an end to the degradation and violence inflicted upon women and children, and will lead to greater dignity for our country as a whole.

Madam Speaker, 1 found the Hon. Member's speech very interesting. I agree with her that this is an important issue and needs to be discussed now. Like my colleague from Broadview-Greenwood, I think it is good that the Government has brought this issue forward for discussion. I can definitely say that the Conservative Party is bold in bringing this forward. My hon. friend is a feminist and I am sure she has fought to have this issue brought forward. We are all very concerned about it. However, there are a couple of things I would like to raise with her.
She mentioned that she knows what eroticism is. She knows what pornography is. She also mentioned that Madam Speaker knows, but I will not ask her to comment. She mentioned that the courts know. Given that she knows the definitions, which seems to be the heart of the dispute, why would the attorneys-general, who will be in part responsible for dealing with this question of definition, raise such serious concerns? They will be involved with those courts which my hon. friend says should be so clear on the definitions.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my thanks to my colleague from Yukon (Mrs. McLaughlin). Of course, like all the women who sit in this House, we are the first ones to be interested and concerned by that question since we have been the models, we are the persons who have been exploited over all those years. Now my colleague is saying that the Attorney General will be responsible for the definition. Somebody has to be responsible. The role of Parliament is to legislate, courts are there to interpret the laws, and I think I can safely assume that Parliament could amend the definitions if it ever becomes clear
November 30, 1987

that the Attorney General is unable to define clearly a precise problem. As 1 have said earlier, I have faith in our court system, and in Canadian men and women. 1 am sure that we will eventually agree upon a definition of erotica and pornography.

Madam Speaker, I would like to congratulate my colleague on the very fine way in which she articulated the problem and the challenges which the Conservative Government faces. She gives the Government full marks for being bold in this area as should the entire Parliament and as do, I believe, the people of Canada.
1 have to take exception with comments which I have heard made by members of the New Democratic and Liberal Parties that this measure is not finding wide support among the people of Canada. That is absolutely wrong. Much of the support for this Bill, I admit, is not coming from lobby groups but from individual Canadians who recognize pornography when they see it in the corner store and who want something done about it.
When I heard the allegation that this concern about pornography and the Government's response to it was only something which the Tories had dreamed up and that it did not have widespread support, I checked my mail of the past week on the subject of Bill C-54.
A Mr. Ed Woodman from Niagara Falls concludes his letter to me of November 10 as follows:
I hope and pray, sir, that you will throw your whole weight behind this 100
per cent.
I also received a letter this past week from Mary Beasley of Shakespeare Avenue in Niagara-on-the-Lake. She said:
I would like to state my support for the passage of Bill C-54, as I am
strongly opposed to pornography. This legislation is long overdue.
Among other things she says:
I wish my voice to be heard and to count in this battle.
I can tell Mrs. Beasley and other constituents such as Phil LoForti and Erwin Fluisbrink that they are being listened to in this debate. The Government is again bringing forward the kind of legislation for which the people have been asking. We are not passing the buck as has so often been the case in justice-related issues.
My colleague referred to the prostitution Bill which was before the House. That is another example of where the buck was passed. The previous Government talked and talked about how concerned it was with the subject. However, it was the Conservative Government that finally did something about it. It gave tools to the law enforcement agencies to do something about the problem of street soliciting. The same is true in this case. Anyone can criticize, saying that they do not like the definition or that it is too narrow, too broad, too vague, too
Criminal Code
this, or too that. However, as my colleague has said, we have had the courage to go ahead and try to do something about this problem.
The people who are not part of lobbying groups, who are not being financed by the Government, are being listened to. This legislation is a response to the very genuine concern of people about pornography. I would again like to congratulate my colleague and invite any further comment she might have.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my colleague is right. The great majority of Canadians have been waiting too long for this Bill. I have received many phone calls from constituents who were sick and tired of being obliged to take pornographic videos away from their young children. The 15 or 16-year-old children do not understand why these videos are available at the store if they are harmful.
During the leaders' debate in 1984 the three leaders agreed that the Government of Canada had a responsibility to stop the illegal entrance of pornography and the degradation of women and children. The Government has decided to act and I am proud to be a member of the Government which has addressed this problem. The women and children of Canada will finally regain dignity in our great country.

Madam Speaker, 1 rise to speak on this most important Bill dealing with a most important subject. When Calvin Coolidge was President of the United States he was asked by his wife who was unable to attend church that morning, "What did the Minister say, Cal? What did he talk about?" Coolidge, who was known as a man of very few words, said, "Sin". She asked, "What did he say about it, Cal?" Coolidge's reply was, "He's agin it".
I think we are all against sin. We are certainly concerned about the recent avalanche of pornographic material, especially as it becomes harder and harder in its depiction of violence, whether on television, in magazines, or what have you. We are alarmed and horrified by the pornographic and sexual abuse of children.
Various things have been said about one party and another. However, in order to counter the deluge of material which has been increasing over the years we must ensure that we pass legislation which will stamp out the proliferation of violent and degrading sexual material, especially that which applies to women and children.
Brutality, bestiality, degradation and violence are regarded by us all as abhorrent. We must try to prevent that which will educate or in any way influence people to perform violent acts or to accept them in a human and decent society. We are, therefore, in agreement with those steps which will move in that direction.
We must ensure that in doing this we do not create legislation which achieves the goal we want while bringing those goals into disrepute and making the Bill itself an objection.

November 30, 1987
Criminal Code
That is the task of every Member of the House of Commons. It is not merely the goal of the Opposition, although it is certainly our special role to study legislation and pick it apart in an effort to ensure that it is good legislation. There are parts of this Bill which concern librarians and the artistic community. There are parts of the Bill that concern churches and religious leaders. They are not happy with aspects of this Bill. It is their responsibility to communicate their concerns and make sure that the Bill is good. Personally, I must call attention to the clause which deals with the subject of erotica. Clause 1 of the Bill states:
'erotica' means any visual matter a dominant characteristic of which is the depiction, in a sexual context or for the purpose of the sexual stimulation of the viewer...
It then lists certain parts of the anatomy.
Clause 159.7 then states:
Every person who displays any erotica in a way that is visible to a member of the public in a public place, unless the public must, in order to see the erotica, pass a prominent warning notice advising of the nature of the display therein or unless the erotica is hidden by a barrier or is covered by an opaque wrapper, is guilty of an offence punishable on summary conviction.
It is provisions such as these which concern the libraries, the religious community and the artistic community. They ask whether we are dealing with those things such as hard core pornography that we want to stop, or also including in the Bill such an omnibus list of concerns that it will create a backlash and a loss of respect for this legislation.
I hope the committee will examine this Bill very carefully and make sure that the objectives I have outlined will be achieved and, at the same time, eliminate those concerns so that, by being so puritanical or unenforcible in its nature, this Bill will not earn derision rather than respect.
We all know the dangerous results of the Bill that was passed in the name of temperance. That Bill which in effect imposed prohibition did not cease the use of alcohol as hoped, or bring about temperance in alcohol, but stimulated its use in the United States far beyond anything it had been before. That Bill brought about waves of crime, gang wars, smuggling and tax evasion. That Bill which was supposed to bring temperance left in its wake a whole way of life that was violent. It brought about total disrespect for the law. That is certainly what we must avoid. We must not pass legislation that will bring about such a backlash from the general public that it will be merely regarded as a joke.
We must deal with this matter with respect and great care. For example, we must recognize that 5 per cent or less of the pornographic materials to which we all object is created here in Canada. Over 95 per cent of it is created in the United States or transshipped through the United States. When we consider free trade, let us hope that this will not be more of the free trade that we want. I hope we will remember that not all blessings come from the south when we think of what it means to have open borders.
We also must consider whose responsibility it is to prove someone's innocence or guilt. The committee must carefully consider the question of responsibility for proving whether or not this law has been contravened. There must be due process and respect for the ancient rule and view of British common law that a person is innocent until proven guilty. We must not create a situation in which it is up to the artist, for example, to prove his or her innocence. I do not know that anyone could regard themselves as artists and feel free in any society if they were afraid there would be laws in this country making one guilty until proven innocent.
I hope the House will make a radical examination of these matters when the Bill goes to committee, to ensure that mistakes are not made again.
I refer to Bill C-114 which was known as the Crosbie Bill. The Government presented this Bill to the House for passage. However, not only did the Opposition and many people throughout the country object to the Bill, Members of the Government benches, in private and in caucus, urged that the Bill not be passed because it was bad legislation.
It is not necessarily correct that the Government has taken positive action simply because it has brought forward a Bill to finally deal with a subject. If the Government is so incompetent in drafting a bill to deal with a particular problem that it cannot get the support of its own benches, obviously it had better take a hard look at this Bill.
There are many people who definitely want to stamp out every form of hard core pornography, which is evil, and at the same time want to make sure that our freedom of speech is maintained. Our artists must not feel that they live in a country where they cannot create a society that will bring about sensitivity and respect for the love of people and their relationships. We must ensure that that legislation does not attack love, sexuality or the artistic depiction of love in some way.
I believe the committee should analyse some present forms of art that are acceptable to Canadians to see whether this Bill will pass the test. Let the committee be absolutely sure that the language will eliminate what we want while respecting the values of our society, especially for education.
Let us also be sure that our children will be educated safely and adequately due to the dangers of AIDS, sexual diseases and so on. We must pass legislation that does not merely supply a platform for someone to make a point. Let us have legislation that is worded in a way that good educational material for children about sexual behaviour, sexual relationships and explanations will not be ruled out and make us in the House of Commons look absurd.
I see my time has expired at this point, or at least that my time is up.
November 30, 1987

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   CANADA ELECTIONS ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   CANADA ELECTIONS ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
that Bill C-268, an Act to amend the Canada Elections Act (non-listed electors), be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Madam Speaker, I would like to begin my comments by suggesting that often many Canadians take our democratic privileges for granted. When one considers the turn-out in federal, provincial, regional and local elections, one is somewhat disappointed by the relatively small turn-out which would indicate that many Canadians simply do not take the opportunities presented to them to cast their ballots for the candidates of their choice. We have been reminded of the precious value of what we have in Canada, what we have known for many decades, by the recent developments in Haiti. For years and years its people have not had an opportunity to express their views of those who would govern them. The attempt at a return to democracy in Haiti has resulted in terrible bloodshed and harassment of voters by armed thugs and we have seen the democratic process which was attempting to reawaken in Haiti set back for some time.
It is interesting, when we consider that the United Nations identifies about 165 countries in the world, how many of these countries actually practice a democratic way of government as we do in Canada. How many of these countries actually hold free and open elections based on the principle of universality and on the right of an election to be called regularly so that the people of these countries have an opportunity to evaluate those who govern them and decide whether they want to change or continue with the status quo? Out of those 165 countries, less than 30 countries actually practice a democratic system as we know it in Canada. That really brings home to us just how precious is our democratic way of life.
Today's Private Members' Bill is really two-fold. It recognizes this precious way of government in our country, and it offers three changes to the way people cast their votes so as to make our system perhaps more equitable and able to provide a fair opportunity to more electors.
I want to begin by reminding Members that in the last federal election, at the last minute, so to speak, 510,000 people
Canada Elections Act
had their names added to the voters' list. This gives us an idea of how accurate and thorough the normal procedure is for assembling those voters' lists. For one reason or another nearly one-half a million Canadians found themselves off that list and had to take steps at the last minute to have their names placed on the voters' list, either successfully or unsuccessfully.
This modest Bill attempts to do three things. It attempts, first, to allow urban voters to be sworn in and be able to vote on election day. This is a privilege, of course, that we have had in rural Canada virtually from the very beginning because in times past it was recognized that as high as 80 per cent of the residents in Canada were rural dwellers, and the assumption was that it would be difficult to find everyone at home, or to make the necessary calls to place everyone on the voters' list. In order to provide a sense of fairness, on election day, if one was living in what was designated as rural Canada, one could be sworn in, have one's name placed on the voters' list and be able to place one's ballot. Such is not the case in urban Canada. With more than 80 per cent of Canadians living in urban centres, it is time, I feel, that that same opportunity be offered to urban voters.
I suppose in sociological terms, one can make the case that the modern city often makes it difficult to enumerate voters because of the transient nature of the population. People are regularly moving, particularly in some parts of our cities, and I am thinking primarily of those living in rented accommodation. There are incredibly high levels of transition with apartment dwellers. I know from talking to some of my colleagues in the House of Commons that there is 100 per cent turnover from one election to another for a lion's share of their constituents which indicates the rather transitory nature of many of our voters.
The days when everyone knew their neighbours and could offer suggestions and assistance to help urban voters get on the election rolls are unfortunately passed for many Canadians who now live in virtual anonymity. They do not even know the person in the next apartment, in the next condominium or, in many cases, in the next house. In sociological terms one could make the case that the same opportunity ought to be offered to those living in our urban areas as traditionally provided to those living in the rural areas.
A second provision in the Bill allows candidates and canvassers to have entry to apartment buildings, condominiums or hotels which have in place a "no soliciting" policy. I recognize that a number of provinces through various pieces of legislation, usually respecting the Landlord and Tenants Act, provide this opportunity and in a sense prohibit owners of apartment blocks, hotels and condominiums from stopping canvassers and candidates from entering buildings to go door to door in order to offer the traditional presentations that we find during a federal election campaign. However, there are some provinces where this provision does not exist and I feel that because of the federal Government's constitutional control over the electoral process, it would make sense to complement what some provincial legislators have already done in the past,

November 30, 1987
Canada Elections Act
and that is to provide this access. I think in the tradition of the federal electoral process, it ought to be part of our Act as well.
I think we have all encountered, and it is actually prohibited by law, harassment of canvassers and candidates from certain apartment blocks where the owner perhaps simply does not like the individual involved or does not want to present any kind of harassment to his or her renters or those staying in the apartment, hotel or condo. This would simply make it impossible for one to deny the access of a candidate or canvasser to that particular building.
Although I do not see this as a significant problem, I think we have all encountered it, this would simply set the record straight so that every Canadian, regardless of where they live in a community, will have access to canvassers or to candidates. This information, of course, is necessary. We assume that in the democratic process, the voter will cast his or her ballot as a result of informed decision making. That requires them to have access to canvassers and access to candidates. It is also important for the canvasser or candidate to have access to all of the voters for their files and to complete their information and, of course, to present themselves face to face with the person who will eventually be casting the ballot. It is an attempt at fairness in order that all Canadians, regardless of where they live, will have access to that same level of information.
The last part of the Bill is to allow travellers and students who are temporarily resident outside of Canada to vote in federal elections. Canadians are among the most travelled people in the world. On a per capita basis we are the world's travellers. In the summertime Canadians are well known for travelling abroad. During the cold winter months the mass exodus into the sun belt is now a Canadian phenomenon. If an election is called in the summer, as was the last federal election, or in the depths of winter, large numbers of Canadian travellers will be outside the country, to say nothing of the students involved.
One of the most positive aspects of our student population is the increasing numbers of Canadian students, young and not so young, who are taking the opportunity to pursue their studies outside of Canada, to spend a year or two at other institutions of higher learning and take advantage of opportunities in schools and institutions abroad. We ought to take steps in order that we do not deny those people the opportunity to cast a ballot on election day.
In the Canada Elections Act steps have been taken to provide that opportunity to those serving in the Armed Forces, and those working abroad in External Affairs offices. They are able to register and cast their ballots in a federal election. This Bill suggests that the same opportunity ought to be provided to Canadians who can swear their residency in Canada, indicate and demonstrate that they are citizens of the country, and if they are students studying abroad or Canadians who are
travelling abroad, that they will not be disenfranchised or lose their right to cast their ballot in a federal election.
In a nutshell, that is what Bill C-268 is all about. It is an attempt to remedy three problem areas. As parliamentarians those areas are not particularly new to us. On a number of occasions the Chief Electoral Officer of Canada has brought these and many other problems to the attention of parliamentarians. When one considers that hopefully a winter election is in the offing, the Government will see fit to call an election on the free trade, and that will mean a winter election when a lot of Canadians are outside of the country and a lot of students will be caught outside the country.

speechtext: Which winter?

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   CANADA ELECTIONS ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
I hear that other Members are listening. If it is not a winter election, possibly it will be a summer election. But at whatever time, there will be large numbers of Canadians caught outside of the country and denied the right to cast their ballot.
I hope that Hon. Members will see fit to send this Bill to a legislative committee for thorough examination and study. Hopefully it will be passed at the following sitting, and we can get on with removing some of those more obvious inequalities and injustices when it comes to casting our votes in a federal election.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   CANADA ELECTIONS ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I think that the House should be indebted to the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) for bringing this Bill to the House. It is an important Bill. It deals with issues that the House must from time to time deal with, and that is the Canada Elections Act. As the Hon. Member pointed out, there will be an election one day. We would not want to have that election without adding four people to the representation from British Columbia in this House. I am surprised that the Member pointed to a winter election. Any election would have to be after there was an opportunity for a representation to the extent of the way it ought to be bearing in mind the last census.
I wish to address the issue in Clause 2 of the Bill which deals with the question of canvassers for a candidate or the candidate himself being able to enter rented or condominium premises. The Bill also mentions hotels. I point out to the House, and my friend, that in a number of provinces that right has already been given. The reason it is given is that under our Constitution the provinces are responsible for the property and civil rights in the province. The provinces of Newfoundland, New Brunswick, Quebec, Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, and British Columbia have provided that not only in provincial elections or municipal elections which are within the purview of the province, but also in federal elections, candidates and canvassers are entitled to enter and bring forth the necessary messages to let people know that an election is on, and present their candidate's viewpoint. That is a very important right.
November 30, 1987

Obviously, apartment houses are private places. To give someone the right to break in or enter private premises and wander the corridors and do the things that candidates or canvassers do in an election, knock on doors and disturb people and ask for a vote, to some extent is interfering with privacy. But it is an important interference of privacy. I think the House would agree that it is important.
The House would also agree that perhaps we do not have the right constitutionally to insist in the Canada Elections Act that we can break down the privacy of private property, as that property is within the jurisdictional confines of the provinces.
If, in bringing this Bill to committee, we find that we cannot go ahead with Clause 2, perhaps we can use the pressure of the House to persuade the provinces of Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, and Alberta to extend the rights that other provinces have given people who are campaigning in federal elections.
I wish to point out that the Province of Alberta extends that permission to people who are campaigning in provincial elections, but not in federal elections. It would not be much of an extension to extend the benefit for federal elections.
The question of whether canvassers should be able to enter hotels is another matter that ought to be looked at very closely, and if people in hotels should even be enumerated. Normally hotels are places where people stay for a short period of time. There are certain requirements of being resident at the time an election is called, and actually being resident in the hotel and not just temporarily staying there. The question boils down to how is a hotel defined. Perhaps the Bill is deficient in that definition. Surely, it is not the right to enter any hotel. Surely, it is not the right to enter the Westin Hotel and wander up and down the halls knocking on every door and saying, "I want your vote". That hotel is there for people who come to this city to do business, and it is not a residential hotel where people stay week after week or month after month and use it as their permanent residence from which they will vote. There must be some definition work done on this Bill, or perhaps the word "hotel" removed from the Bill. Certainly, the committee can do that.
I do not wish to take up a great deal of time on the matter. I think it is good that the Hon. Member has brought the Bill to the House.
Turning to the section dealing with the special voting right, I think that matter has been before the House previously. Certainly it has been brought to the attention of the House by people studying the Canada Elections Act. Of course the question is: What about people travelling abroad or who are only temporarily abroad? It seems that to extend the voting ability to people who are just temporarily abroad would be most improper and most difficult. Perhaps proxy voting systems might better solve the problem. However, to have some provision where people could register their vote with an
Canada Elections Act
embassy or consulate would seem to be very difficult, particularly people who are away from the country on holiday. Clearly people who are away on a long-term stay, temporarily no longer resident in Canada or staying outside Canada on a posting, ought to be given some special right to vote in our elections.
Having made those few comments, I commend the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap on a good Bill. I hope that it will go on to committee.

Mir. Marcel Prud'homme (Saint-Denis): Madam Speaker, I would like to join the previous speaker in thanking the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis), since the Bill is in his name, for introducing this Bill on October 6, which means we now have an opportunity to consider his Bill this evening.
Madam Speaker, we know it is only a matter of time, and I hope it will be very soon, before the Government tables Bill C-79, an Act to amend the Canada Elections Act and other Acts in relation thereto. First reading was on June 30, 1987, and I think the Government will be bringing in the Bill for second reading very shortly. I intend to take a very active interest in the proceedings when we consider this Bill.
Meanwhile, the Hon. Member has submitted a number of proposals to the House, and at first glance,-and with my experience of election campaigns, both my own and the campaigns of others, which should total about 100, with at least eight of my own-I believe there are a number of items here to which we can say yes immediately. I hope that if we do not reach some kind of agreement this evening, we will be able to reconsider the Hon. Member's suggestions when the Government brings in its own Bill very shortly.
I agree it is very annoying when you get people who arrive at the polling station on election day who, the day before, suddenly realized they were not on the voters' list. I must admit it is very frustrating, both for the elector and often for the political organizations who urged these people to get out and vote during the election campaign. But there is also the question whether this has to be left until the very last day, until election day.
It works all right in small urban centres and in rural areas. Then there is no problem. However, in our cities, many people would think twice about giving this kind of last chance to someone who comes in under the wire, at a time when everybody is busy processing hundreds of voters. Someone will have to decide who is and who is not a voter and swear them in. I think that would unduly delay the process and would also discourage some electors who are already on the list. However, I do feel positive about this proposal.
I know that Bill C-79, the Bill the Government intends to table very shortly, contains a reference to this problem, since so far, we can add electors to the list up to the seventeenth day before the election. I believe the Government is proposing in

November 30, 1987
Canada Elections Act
Bill C-79 to extend the revision period until the 12th day, including a specific clause that provides for the registration of a voter. That is in Bill C-79. Now, with this Bill, we could . .. and I am all for it, not that I am against what the Hon. Member is offering us, but the Government goes so far as saying that until three days before, that is until the Friday before the vote, it will be possible to go to the office of the returning officer in order to add to the electoral list the name of the people who might have been left out during the revision and who might come up at the last minute.
So I think the Hon. Member, who is a reasonable gentleman, will be interested to discuss it further when we deal with Bill C-79, an act to amend the Canada Elections Act and other acts in relation thereto.
To this day, I am satisfied that there is at least a disposition to act. I wanted to put forward an amendment myself but there we have a proposal by the Government to extend the period until Friday. That is a considerable improvement, especially for people who live in urban areas. Because my colleagues and I, during the electoral campaign, we keep finding people who are not on the list and it is very frustating not to be able to have them added. At least, we know that we will be able to have them added to the list up until the Friday before the election. So whether it is the Friday before or the very same day, 1 believe there is not much difference between what the Hon. Member is proposing, what we have been requesting for a long time and what should be done. There will be a possibility when the day comes to combine all the various proposals.
The second proposal of the Hon. Member would also be a source of difficulty as some building owners forbid any entry because the tenants are senior citizens, people who are afraid of seeing so many visitors circulate in their building, as the previous speaker pointed out. There also, I am rather inclined to agree with my colleague. However, I would like us to be able to examine all implications very carefully.
We all know what it means and how difficult it is to visit certain large apartment buildings in Montreal, Toronto or Vancouver. There could be twelve candidates coming once, twice or three times. This could mean up to thirty-six visits by people, either by themselves or with others, to campaign in a building. There are problems, but it is always possible to find solutions. For my part, I am an optimist. We can look at all that later on when we examine the legislation which the Government should bring back very soon. The Hon. Member is certainly better informed than I am about that as he is the House Leader of his party. I imagine, however, that Bill C-79 will be referred to a committee in the near future. If this Bill does not pass today, I hope that he will be in the House then to go over all his proposals.
Therefore, there are no major objections except for the fact that this will create difficulties. We shall have to look at a way to appease the fears that many people may have in seeing all kinds of visitors in their buildings, especially in the major
centres, where people have a greater tendency to be scared. I do not blame them. It is a major problem in the downtown areas where there are big buildings in which no strangers are admitted. But how can we defend democracy if we cannot talk to people? It would be appropriate to have a lengthy debate on this issue.
The third proposal of the Hon. Member, the last one, after which I shall sit down and let others speak as provided by our rules, aims at allowing travellers and students who are temporarily residing abroad to vote in a general election, just like the members of the Canadian Armed Forces and public servents posted are allowed to do.
However, I forsee problems in this regard also. For twenty years, we have been looking at ways to make it possible for the greatest number of Canadians to vote. How can we do that? Members of the Armed Forces are registered annually, and so are public servants on foreign postings, but it would be difficult to do the same for students and travellers.
I am certain that our discussions will be lengthy when the Government Bill is being considered. In fact, the Bill includes a whole section on the right to vote of others than the military and public servants. This raises enormous difficulties. The Hon. Member is aware of that. Where will we stop? Students in Canada, that's understandable. Students abroad, that's also understandable, but is their status permanent? We always have much sympathy for students. As for Canadian citizens travelling abroad, we do not know. Once you open the door in the case of travellers, the next time you probably would want to open it for . . . As a matter of fact, a provision in the Government's Bill makes it possible to extend the right to vote to people temporarily residing outside Canada without losing their citizenship. But as you know, their situation is similar to that of people coming to Ottawa to work for a while. If you keep talking long enough about the people who are in Ottawa on a temporary basis, you suddenly realize that they are here on a permanent basis. This will create difficulties.
I know that in the Bill introduced by the Government, it is difficult to decide when to say yes or no? Personally, I have no final opinion on this for reasons which I will explain when we deal with this Bill. I prefer not to indicate my final opinion, because I intend to be very actively involved when the House considers Bill C-79. The reason I wanted to speak to this Bill was to show the difficulty we will have to face, but there is no doubt that it will be possible to follow through with our colleague's number one proposal.
As far as the second proposal is concerned, we will have to decide how we can assure the safety of people living in a building while carrying out our duties during an election campaign in a democratic society. I share the concern of my Hon. friend on this.
As to the third proposal, we will consider it more thoroughly soon, because it represents something which I feel is new, complex, but we want to extend the right to vote to the
November 30, 1987

greatest number of Canadians. With his proposal, therefore, our Hon. friend has given us food for thought.
